title: Hotel Registration in Nepal Through Foreign Investment
content:
Opening a hotel in Nepal looks straightforward from the outside. The sector is open to foreign investment, tourism is a national priority, and the demand for well-run accommodation is steady. What first-time investors underestimate is the number of separate approvals a hotel needs, and the fact that they sit with different authorities. The result is that an investment can be approved and still not be ready to open.

This guide sets out the approvals a hotel needs, in the order they should be secured, so your opening date is a plan rather than a hope.

Quick answer

This guide covers the complete process of registering a hotel in Nepal through foreign investment, including the legal framework (Tourism Act 2035, Hotel Lodge Restaurant Bar Rules 2038, FITTA 2019, FITTR 2021, IEA 2020), why hotels are open to 100% foreign ownership (unlike travel agencies), the 8 hotel classification categories (General Tourist Standard through 5-Star Deluxe), minimum FDI threshold (NPR 20 million), the full 10-step process from DOI FDI approval through DoT hotel classification, the Standard Fixation Committee’s role, hotel construction standards, star classification criteria and fees (NPR 5,000 to NPR 60,000), the 5-year classification renewal requirement, NRB investment recording and profit repatriation rules, post-registration compliance obligations including semi-annual reporting, tax incentives for hotel investment, and 12 FAQs. Researched and verified against 2025 regulations by the Pluto Associates legal team, Kathmandu.

Introduction: Why Nepal’s Hotel Sector Is One of Its Best Foreign Investment Opportunities

Nepal’s tourism industry is one of the country’s most strategically important economic sectors. With over 1.2 million tourists visiting annually, a landscape that includes eight of the world’s ten highest mountains, world-heritage listed cities, ancient Buddhist and Hindu pilgrimage sites, and national parks of extraordinary biodiversity, Nepal has the natural and cultural raw material to sustain a hospitality industry of far greater scale than currently exists.

The gap between what Nepal has to offer and the quality and quantity of accommodation available to exploit it represents one of the most significant investment opportunities in South Asia. NPR 350 billion has already been invested in Nepal’s hotel industry, but demand continues to outpace supply, particularly in the mid-range and luxury segments, and in secondary destinations beyond Kathmandu.

The good news for foreign investors: Unlike travel agencies and trekking companies, which are on FITTA’s Negative List and closed to foreign ownership, hotels are explicitly open to foreign direct investment. A foreign national or foreign company can own 100% of a hotel in Nepal without requiring a Nepali joint venture partner. This is a significant distinction that makes the hospitality sector one of the most accessible for international capital in Nepal’s entire economy.

The process of establishing a foreign-invested hotel in Nepal is a multi-stage regulatory journey that spans the Department of Industry (for FDI approval), the Office of Company Registrar (for company incorporation), Nepal Rastra Bank (for capital recording and foreign exchange compliance), and the Department of Tourism (for hotel registration and star classification). Each stage has its own documents, timelines, and requirements. This guide walks through every step.

“More than NPR 350 billion has been invested in Nepal’s hotel industry. Yet the gap between tourist demand and quality accommodation supply remains enormous, particularly in mid-range and luxury segments. For foreign investors with hospitality expertise and capital, Nepal’s hotel sector offers an opportunity that is difficult to find elsewhere in South Asia.”

Legal Framework: Laws Governing Hotel Investment and Registration in Nepal

A foreign-invested hotel in Nepal sits at the intersection of investment law, tourism law, and company law. Understanding each layer is essential before committing capital or approaching any government office.

Law / Instrument

Year

Relevance to Hotel Registration

Tourism Act (Paryatan Ain)

2035 (1978)

Primary tourism legislation. Section 10 governs hotel registration. Section 11 establishes the Standard Fixation Committee for hotel classification. Section 47 requires semi-annual reporting by registered hotels. Defines the legal basis for all hotel licensing in Nepal.

Hotel, Lodge, Restaurant, Bar and Tourist Guide Rules (HLRB Rules)

2038 (1981)

Detailed operational rules implementing the Tourism Act for the hospitality sector. Rule 3 sets out the hotel registration application procedure. Rule 5 requires star hotels to adhere to standards fixed by the Standard Fixation Committee. Defines minimum facility requirements for each hotel category.

Hotel Standard (Hotelको Maan)

2077 (2020)

Updated classification criteria for all hotel categories. Specifies the exact minimum standards, room count, bathroom ratios, food service, safety facilities, accessibility, for each star category from General Tourist Standard through 5-Star Deluxe.

Tourism Industry Service Delivery Directory

2070 (2013)

Section 83 requires star-rated hotels to renew their DoT classification every 5 years. Section 83(2) mandates renewal application before expiry.

Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA)

2019 (2076 BS)

Primary FDI law. Hotels are NOT on the Negative List, foreign investment in hotels is permitted, including 100% foreign ownership. Governs FDI approval process, minimum investment threshold (NPR 20 million), investor rights, and repatriation of profits.

Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Rules (FITTR)

2021 (2077 BS)

Implements FITTA. Provides procedural details on FDI application, document requirements, the investment schedule (three-stage capital injection timeline), and automatic approval route for investments up to NPR 500 million.

Industrial Enterprises Act (IEA)

2076 (2020)

Requires industry registration after company incorporation. Hotels qualify as service industries under the IEA and must be registered at the Department of Industry. Operations must commence within 1 year of industry registration.

Companies Act (Kampani Ain)

2063 (2006)

Governs company incorporation at the OCR. All hotel businesses must be incorporated as companies before approaching any other regulatory authority.

Nepal Rastra Bank Act + FERA

2058 / 2019

Nepal Rastra Bank regulates foreign currency transactions. All FDI capital must be remitted through official banking channels and recorded with NRB within 6 months of injection. Profit repatriation requires NRB approval and tax clearance.

Income Tax Act

2058 (2002)

Hotel income is subject to corporate income tax. Special tax incentives apply for hotels in certain geographic areas. PAN registration and annual tax filing are mandatory.

⚖️ Key Distinction from Travel Agencies: The FITTA 2019 Negative List explicitly includes travel agencies, trekking agencies, and tour operators, these are closed to foreign investment. Hotels are NOT on this Negative List. A foreign investor can own 100% of a hotel company in Nepal without a Nepali partner. This is the single most important legal fact for any foreign investor evaluating Nepal’s hospitality sector.

Hotel Classification in Nepal: What Category Will Your Hotel Fall Into?

Before beginning any registration process, the foreign investor must understand Nepal’s hotel classification system. Your hotel’s category determines which specific construction standards apply, what facilities are mandatory, what fees you pay at the Department of Tourism, and how you will be marketed to incoming tourists.

📌 Classification Is Mandatory: Every hotel operating in Nepal must obtain a classification from the Department of Tourism’s Standard Fixation Committee before opening to guests. Operating without DoT classification is illegal under the Tourism Act 2035 and attracts penalties and forced closure. The classification also determines your legal right to call your property a “5-Star” or any other rated hotel, using a star rating without DoT classification is a misrepresentation.

3.1 The Standard Fixation Committee

The Standard Fixation Committee is a body established by the Government of Nepal under Section 11 of the Tourism Act 2035. It is responsible for recommending the classification or registration of hotels, lodges, restaurants, resorts, and bars as tourism standards. The Committee inspects proposed or completed hotel properties against the criteria established in the Hotel Standard 2077 and makes classification recommendations to the Department of Tourism.

For a new hotel project, the Standard Fixation Committee inspection typically occurs after construction is complete and the hotel is substantially ready for operation. The investor cannot receive the final hotel classification certificate until this inspection has been conducted and the Committee is satisfied that all applicable standards are met.

Foreign Investment Eligibility: Who Can Invest and How Much Is Required?

4.1 Eligible Foreign Investors

  • Foreign nationals: Any foreign national above 18 years of age from a country with which Nepal has diplomatic relations can invest in a hotel in Nepal.
  • Foreign companies: Any company registered and operating in a foreign country can invest in a Nepali hotel, subject to FITTA 2019 compliance.
  • 100% foreign ownership: Hotels are fully open to 100% foreign ownership. A Nepali joint venture partner is not legally required, though many foreign investors choose to partner with Nepali investors for local market knowledge and relationship networks.
  • No country-specific exclusions: There is no list of excluded countries for hotel investment in Nepal, subject to any applicable government sanctions or orders.

4.2 Minimum Investment Threshold

Under FITTA 2019, the minimum foreign investment in Nepal is NPR 20,000,000 (NPR 20 million, approximately USD 150,000) for most sectors. For hotels, this represents a very low floor relative to the actual cost of establishing any commercially viable hotel property. In practice, even a modest 3-star hotel in Kathmandu requires investment well above the NPR 20 million threshold.

✅ Automatic Route Advantage: For hotel investments up to NPR 500 million (approximately USD 3.8 million), the Automatic Route at the DoI is available, with a statutory 7-day processing window. This significantly accelerates the FDI approval timeline for small and mid-size hotel projects compared to the standard review process.

4.3 Forms of Foreign Investment Recognized Under FITTA 2019

Foreign investment in a Nepali hotel can take several forms, all recognized under Section 2(j) of FITTA 2019:

  • Equity investment: Purchase of shares in a Nepali hotel company. The most common FDI form.
  • Reinvestment of earnings: Reinvesting dividends or profits generated by the hotel back into the business.
  • Loan capital: Loans from foreign lenders to the hotel company, subject to NRB approval for foreign borrowing.
  • Technology transfer: Contribution of proprietary hotel management systems, brand licenses, or operational know-how in exchange for equity or royalties.
  • Franchise arrangements: International hotel brand franchise agreements (e.g. Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt franchise) constitute a form of technology/brand transfer recognized under FITTA.

Complete 10-Step Registration Process for a Foreign-Invested Hotel

The hotel registration process through foreign investment is the most complex business registration journey in Nepal’s tourism sector. It involves more regulatory authorities than any other tourism business, because it combines the FDI approval and investment recording framework with the hotel-specific construction, inspection, and classification requirements. The steps must be followed in the correct sequence, there are no shortcuts.

STEP 1 Prepare the Investment Proposal and Feasibility Study

Before approaching any government office, prepare a comprehensive investment proposal and feasibility study for the proposed hotel. This is not a formality, it is a critical working document that the Department of Industry and, for large projects, the Investment Board Nepal will evaluate as part of the FDI approval process.

The investment proposal must include:

  1. Project background and investment rationale
  2. Detailed description of the proposed hotel (location, category, room count, facilities)
  3. Land ownership or lease arrangement details
  4. Total project cost and capital structure (equity vs. debt breakdown)
  5. Foreign investment amount and source of funds
  6. Technical aspects, construction plan, architectural design overview, HVAC, safety systems
  7. Market analysis, target customer segments, occupancy projections, revenue forecasts
  8. Five-year financial projections (income statement, balance sheet, cash flow)
  9. Employment generation plan (Nepali and foreign staff)
  10. Environmental and social impact assessment (if required for the location)

✅ Location Due Diligence: Before finalizing your hotel project, verify the land use zoning regulations for your proposed site. Not all land in Nepal is zoned for hotel/commercial development. Kathmandu Valley, Pokhara, and Chitwan have specific zoning plans. Consult the relevant municipality and Department of Urban Development before purchasing or leasing land for hotel construction.

ℹ️ Timeline: Investment proposal preparation: 4-8 weeks with professional financial modellers and legal advisors.

STEP 2 Obtain FDI Approval from the Department of Industry

The first government interaction for a foreign-invested hotel is with the Department of Industry (DoI) at the One Stop Service Centre (OSSC), Tripureshwor, Kathmandu. Submit the FDI application through the DoI’s online portal (imis.doind.gov.np) or in person at the OSSC. The OSSC brings together representatives from multiple government agencies, DoI, OCR, IRD, NRB, under one roof to streamline the FDI approval process.

Documents required for DoI FDI approval:

  1. Prescribed FDI application form (from the OSSC)
  2. Comprehensive project proposal and feasibility study
  3. Bio-data (personal details) of the foreign investor(s)
  4. Copy of foreign investor’s passport
  5. Certificate of Incorporation of the foreign investing entity (with apostille or embassy authentication)
  6. Memorandum of Association (MOA) of the foreign investing entity
  7. Financial credibility certificate or audited financial statements of the foreign investing entity (last 3 years)
  8. Board resolution of the foreign investing entity authorizing the Nepal investment
  9. Source of funds declaration
  10. Power of attorney (if filing through a Nepal-based legal representative)

For investments requiring a DoT recommendation (which applies to hotels above a certain project value or in designated tourism areas), the DoI will coordinate with the Department of Tourism and request their letter of approval as part of the FDI evaluation process.

ℹ️ Automatic Route (NPR 20M, 500M): Under Section 15(2) of FITTA, DoI must process complete Automatic Route applications within 7 working days. The DoI issues the FDI Approval Certificate upon successful evaluation.

ℹ️ Standard Route (NPR 500M, 6B): Standard Route applications take 30-45 working days, as they involve more detailed sectoral review.

STEP 3 Incorporate the Company at the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR)

With the DoI FDI Approval Certificate in hand, incorporate the hotel company as a Private Limited Company at the OCR (camis.ocr.gov.np). This company will own and operate the hotel property in Nepal.

The company’s Memorandum of Association must clearly state hotel operations, hospitality services, and tourism accommodation as the company’s primary business objectives. A vague or incorrect MOA can cause rejection at the DoT classification stage.

Documents required for OCR registration:

  1. DoI FDI Approval Certificate (mandatory for any company with foreign shareholders)
  2. Completed CAMIS portal application form
  3. Memorandum of Association (MOA), hotel and hospitality as primary objectives
  4. Articles of Association (AOA)
  5. Passport copies of foreign shareholders (with apostille/authentication)
  6. Citizenship certificates of any Nepali shareholders
  7. Photographs of all shareholders/directors
  8. Proposed registered office address in Nepal
  9. Digital Signature Certificate (DSC) for authenticated submission
  10. OCR registration fee payment receipt

ℹ️ Timeline: OCR company registration: 7-10 working days from complete submission.

STEP 4 PAN and VAT Registration at the Inland Revenue Department

Register the hotel company for a Permanent Account Number (PAN) at the Inland Revenue Department (IRD). VAT registration is also required for hotel businesses. Hotels charge 13% VAT on room rates and food and beverage services.

PAN and VAT registration are free of charge at the IRD. Apply online at ird.gov.np or in person at the IRD office. Submit the OCR Registration Certificate, MOA, AOA, and proof of registered office address.

📌 Tourism Tax: Hotels in Nepal are also subject to the Tourism Service Fee (TSF), which is collected from guests and remitted to the Department of Tourism. The TSF rate varies by hotel category. Compliance with TSF collection and remittance obligations is monitored by the DoT during periodic inspections.

ℹ️ Timeline: PAN and VAT registration: 3-5 working days.

STEP 5 Ward Office Registration and Business Operation Permit

Register with the Ward Office (Wada Karyalaya) of the municipality where the hotel will be located. Submit the OCR Registration Certificate, PAN certificate, and land or lease documentation for the hotel property. The Ward Office may inspect the site before issuing the Business Operation Permit.

For hotel construction projects (as opposed to existing buildings being converted to hotels), the Business Operation Permit may be issued in two stages: an initial permit for construction activity, and a final operational permit once construction is complete and the hotel is ready to receive guests.

ℹ️ Timeline: Ward Office registration: 3-7 working days.

STEP 6 Industry Registration at the Department of Industry

Following company registration, the hotel must be registered as a service industry at the Department of Industry under the Industrial Enterprises Act 2076. This step produces the Industry Registration Certificate, which formally classifies the hotel as an industry in Nepal’s industrial registry.

This step is frequently overlooked by first-time investors but is a mandatory requirement before approaching the Department of Tourism for hotel classification. Submit the OCR Registration Certificate, MOA, AOA, PAN certificate, FDI Approval Certificate, and office/property documentation to the DoI Industry Registration Section.

⚠️ One-Year Commencement Obligation: Under the IEA 2020, hotel companies must commence operations within one year of receiving the Industry Registration Certificate. “Commencement” for a hotel under construction means having an approved construction plan and active construction activity. For operational hotels, it means receiving the first paying guests. Failure to commence within one year can result in cancellation of the Industry Registration Certificate, which in turn affects the DoT classification.

ℹ️ Timeline: Industry registration: 7-10 working days.

STEP 7 Open Corporate Bank Account and Inject Foreign Investment Capital

Open a corporate bank account at any commercial bank in Nepal in the hotel company’s name. The DoI FDI Approval Certificate specifies the approved investment amount and the timeline within which it must be injected.

The foreign investment capital must be remitted from the investor’s home country through official banking channels (SWIFT transfer) into the hotel company’s Nepali corporate bank account. The FITTR 2021 divides the investment injection process into three stages with specified timelines:

  • Stage 1: Initial capital injection within the first prescribed period after approval.
  • Stage 2: Second tranche injection within the second prescribed period.
  • Stage 3: Remaining capital injection within the third prescribed period.

The bank will issue an Investment Inflow Certificate upon receipt of each foreign currency remittance. This certificate is a critical document for the NRB recording step that follows.

✅ Escrow Arrangement: For hotel construction projects, coordinate with your commercial bank on an appropriate capital management structure. Some investors establish an escrow-type arrangement where capital is released in tranches aligned with construction milestones. This requires coordination between the construction contract, the bank, and the investment schedule under FITTR.

STEP 8 Record the Investment with Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB)

Within 6 months of each foreign currency injection, the hotel company must record the investment with Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB). This is a critical compliance step that is often delayed or overlooked by first-time foreign investors, and the consequences are serious.

To record the investment with NRB, submit:

  1. Investment Inflow Certificate from the commercial bank confirming receipt of foreign currency
  2. Share Registry Certificate (Sher Darta Pramaanpatra) from the OCR confirming the shareholding structure
  3. DoI FDI Approval Certificate
  4. OCR Registration Certificate

NRB issues an Investment Recording Certificate (sometimes called an Investment Certificate) confirming that the foreign investment has been officially registered in Nepal’s foreign exchange records. This certificate is essential for future profit repatriation, without it, dividends and capital returns cannot be remitted out of Nepal through official banking channels.

⚠️ 6-Month Recording Deadline: The investment must be recorded with NRB within 6 months of the date the foreign currency was received by the Nepali bank. Missing this deadline does not void the investment, but it complicates future profit repatriation and may require additional regulatory clearance. Set a calendar reminder from the date of each capital injection.

ℹ️ Timeline: NRB recording: 2-3 weeks from submission of complete documents.

STEP 9 Hotel Construction and Standard Fixation Committee Inspection

This is the longest stage, one that has no fixed government processing time because it depends entirely on the time required to construct and fit out the hotel to the standards required for the target classification. For a 3-star hotel, construction typically takes 18 to 36 months. For a 5-star hotel, 36 to 60 months is common.

During the construction phase, the hotel company must ensure that the building design, room sizes, bathroom ratios, common areas, food service facilities, safety systems, accessibility features, and all other physical aspects of the property comply with the standards specified in the Hotel Standard 2077 for the target classification category.

9.1 Pre-Construction Approvals

Before construction begins, obtain all necessary pre-construction approvals from the relevant municipality:

  • Building permit from the relevant municipality’s Engineering Department
  • Environmental impact assessment clearance (if the project exceeds prescribed thresholds)
  • Fire safety clearance from the Nepal Police/Fire Brigade (required before operations)
  • Structural design approval for multi-storey buildings

9.2 The Standard Fixation Committee Inspection

When the hotel is substantially complete and ready for guest occupancy, submit an application to the Department of Tourism requesting a Standard Fixation Committee inspection for classification. The Committee, which includes representatives from the DoT, Nepal Tourism Board, industry associations, and technical experts, inspects the property against the Hotel Standard 2077 criteria for the applied classification.

The Committee evaluates:

  • Room count and room sizes (minimum area requirements per classification)
  • Bathroom and toilet facilities (attached bathroom requirements)
  • Bed and furnishing standards
  • Food and beverage facilities (restaurant, bar standards)
  • Front desk and reception standards
  • Safety and fire safety systems
  • Parking facilities
  • Accessibility features
  • Staff facilities and back-of-house areas
  • Common area standards (lobbies, corridors, elevators)

If the hotel meets the standards for the applied classification, the Committee issues a classification recommendation to the Department of Tourism, which then issues the Hotel Registration and Classification Certificate.

⚠️ Classification vs Construction Standards: Many investors discover after construction is complete that their hotel does not meet all the physical standards required for their target classification. This is expensive and disruptive to remedy post-construction. Engage a hospitality consultant with knowledge of Nepal’s Hotel Standard 2077 during the design phase, not after construction.

STEP 10 Obtain the DoT Hotel Registration and Classification Certificate

Upon receiving a positive classification recommendation from the Standard Fixation Committee, the Department of Tourism issues the Hotel Registration and Classification Certificate. This certificate is the final, definitive authorization that:

  • Registers the hotel as a legally operating tourism accommodation establishment in Nepal
  • Confirms the hotel’s official classification (e.g. 3-Star, 4-Star, 5-Star General, or 5-Star Deluxe)
  • Authorises the hotel to display the classification rating to guests and in marketing materials
  • Authorises the hotel to collect Tourism Service Fees from guests
  • Lists the hotel on the Department of Tourism’s official registry

The hotel classification certificate is valid for 5 years from the date of issuance. It must be renewed before expiry under Section 83 of the Tourism Industry Service Delivery Directory 2070.

✔ Fully Registered and Classified! With the DoT Hotel Registration and Classification Certificate, the hotel is legally registered and authorized to receive guests. Display the certificate prominently in the hotel lobby.

Post-Registration Compliance: Ongoing Obligations for Foreign-Invested Hotels

A registered hotel’s regulatory obligations do not end with the classification certificate. Nepal’s Tourism Act and related regulations impose a comprehensive set of ongoing compliance obligations throughout the hotel’s operational life.

10.1 The Semi-Annual Report: The Most Commonly Missed Obligation

Section 47 of the Tourism Act 2035 requires every registered hotel to submit a detailed periodic report to the Government of Nepal every 6 months. This report covers:

  • Number of guests by nationality and duration of stay
  • Room occupancy rates and revenue data
  • Details of foreign employees (name, designation, remuneration)
  • Details of goods imported under tourism import permits (if applicable)
  • Details of tourism businesses established abroad in connection with the hotel (if any)
  • Any other information the Department of Tourism may request

These reports are the primary data source for Nepal’s official tourism statistics. Hotels that fail to submit these reports face compliance warnings and complications at the 5-year classification renewal stage.

Profit Repatriation: Getting Your Money Back

One of the most important protections under FITTA 2019 for foreign hotel investors is the explicit right to repatriate profits, dividends, and ultimately the original investment capital from Nepal. This right is guaranteed by statute and is enforceable against the Nepal government.

11.1 What Can Be Repatriated

  • Dividends and profits: After payment of all applicable taxes in Nepal (including income tax and any withholding tax on dividends), net dividends can be repatriated to the investor’s home country.
  • Capital gains: Gains from the sale of shares in the hotel company can be repatriated after paying applicable capital gains tax in Nepal.
  • Return of principal: The original investment capital can be repatriated, subject to a general principle that investors should not repatriate principal within 1 year of injection.
  • Technology transfer fees and royalties: If the investment involves a franchise agreement or technology transfer, royalty payments can be repatriated subject to NRB approval of the underlying agreement.

11.2 Repatriation Process

  1. Obtain a tax clearance certificate from the Inland Revenue Department confirming all taxes have been paid
  2. Apply to Nepal Rastra Bank for repatriation approval, submitting the NRB Investment Recording Certificate, tax clearance, and financial statements
  3. NRB reviews the application and approves the repatriation
  4. The hotel’s commercial bank executes the foreign currency remittance upon NRB approval

⚠️ Pre-Condition: The most common reason repatriation applications are rejected or delayed is that the investment was never properly recorded with NRB in the first place. The 6-month recording deadline after each capital injection is not administrative housekeeping, it is the prerequisite for future repatriation. Investors who miss this recording step cannot straightforwardly repatriate profits until the recording situation is regularized.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. Can a foreign national own 100% of a hotel in Nepal?

Yes. Hotels are not on the Negative List of FITTA 2019, which means foreign nationals and foreign companies can own 100% of a hotel company in Nepal. A Nepali joint venture partner is not legally required. This is a critical distinction from travel agencies and trekking companies, which are on the Negative List and closed to foreign investment.

2. What is the minimum foreign investment required to establish a hotel in Nepal?

The minimum foreign investment threshold under FITTA 2019 is NPR 20,000,000 (NPR 20 million, approximately USD 150,000). In practice, even a modest 3-star hotel requires significantly more capital than this threshold. Land acquisition or lease, construction costs, fit-out, and working capital for a commercially viable hotel typically require NPR 5 crore to NPR 50 crore or more depending on the location, category, and scale of the property.

3. How long does the complete registration process take?

The regulatory registration process itself, from DoI FDI approval through DoT hotel classification certificate, takes approximately 3 to 6 months for a completed hotel property that meets all classification standards. However, for a new construction project, the total end-to-end timeline from investment decision to welcoming the first guests is 2.5 to 4 years for a 3-star hotel and 4.5 to 7 years for a 5-star hotel, primarily due to construction time.

4. What is the DoT hotel classification fee for a 5-Star hotel?

The Department of Tourism registration fee for a 5-Star General hotel is NPR 50,000, and for a 5-Star Deluxe hotel is NPR 60,000. Lower category hotels pay correspondingly lower fees: 1-Star (NPR 5,000), 2-Star (NPR 10,000), 3-Star (NPR 20,000), and 4-Star (NPR 30,000). These are government fees payable at the DoT and do not include any construction, legal, or professional advisory costs.

5. How often must a hotel renew its DoT classification?

Under Section 83 of the Tourism Industry Service Delivery Directory 2070, star-rated hotels must renew their DoT classification every 5 years. The renewal application must be submitted before the classification period expires and must include updated compliance documents, proof of continued compliance with the applicable Hotel Standard 2077 criteria, and payment of the renewal fee. A hotel that fails to renew loses the right to display its star classification.

6. Can a foreign investor bring an international hotel brand to Nepal?

Yes. International hotel brand franchise agreements (Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt, IHG, etc.) can be structured as technology transfer agreements under FITTA 2019. The franchise fee and ongoing royalties paid to the international brand constitute a permitted form of technology transfer payment and can be remitted out of Nepal subject to NRB approval of the underlying franchise agreement. Many of Nepal’s newest luxury hotels are operated under international management contracts or franchise agreements.

7. Are there tax incentives for building a hotel in Nepal?

Yes. Nepal offers income tax exemptions and reduced tax rates for hotels in designated mountain tourism areas and tourism development zones, customs duty exemptions on imported hotel construction equipment and materials, and FITTA-guaranteed profit repatriation rights. The specific incentives available depend on the hotel’s location, classification, and the year of commencement of operations. A detailed analysis of available tax incentives should be conducted as part of the pre-investment feasibility study.

8. What happens if the hotel fails the Standard Fixation Committee inspection?

If the Standard Fixation Committee finds that the hotel does not meet the minimum standards for the applied classification, it will issue a report specifying the deficiencies. The investor must address all identified deficiencies and request a re-inspection. There is no automatic reclassification to a lower star category, the investor must either meet the standards for the applied classification or formally reapply for a lower classification category. Addressing structural deficiencies post-construction is significantly more expensive than building to the correct standards from the beginning.

9. Can the hotel employ foreign nationals?

Yes, with restrictions. Hotels can employ qualified foreign nationals in specialist roles (executive chef, general manager, F&B director, etc.) where the required skills are not available locally. Foreign employees require work permits from the Department of Labour and appropriate visas from the Department of Immigration. The preference for Nepali workers in all roles where qualified local candidates are available is a general regulatory expectation, and foreign worker numbers are subject to DoL oversight.

10. Is it possible to convert an existing building into a hotel in Nepal?

Yes, but the conversion must still satisfy all the physical standards required by the Hotel Standard 2077 for the target classification. The Standard Fixation Committee will inspect the converted property against the same criteria as a new-build hotel. Structural modifications, room size compliance, bathroom standards, and fire safety systems are commonly the most challenging aspects of conversion projects. A detailed pre-conversion audit against the Hotel Standard 2077 criteria is essential before committing to a conversion project.

11. What is the Tourism Service Fee (TSF) and how does it work?

The Tourism Service Fee is a government-mandated fee collected by hotels from guests as part of their accommodation billing. The rate varies by hotel classification, higher-rated hotels collect a higher TSF per guest-night. The hotel acts as a collection agent on behalf of the government and is required to remit the collected TSF to the Department of Tourism on a periodic basis. Failure to collect or remit the TSF is a compliance violation subject to penalties. The TSF amounts are specified in the Tourism Act regulations and are updated periodically by the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation.

12. Can a foreign-invested hotel hold land in Nepal?

Yes, with an important qualification. A Nepali-incorporated company, even one that is 100% foreign-owned, can legally own land in Nepal for the purposes of its registered business activities, including hotel operations. Individual foreign nationals, however, cannot directly own land in Nepal. This means the land on which the hotel sits must be owned or leased by the Nepali company (not directly by the foreign individual investor), which is the standard structure for all foreign-invested hotel projects in Nepal.

Conclusion: Nepal’s Hotel Sector Is Ready for International Investment

Nepal’s hospitality sector sits at a genuinely exciting inflection point. The natural and cultural assets are extraordinary. The tourism demand is real, growing, and increasingly coming from high-value markets. The investment framework, 100% foreign ownership permitted, strong statutory profit repatriation guarantees, meaningful tax incentives in priority areas, and a government that has publicly committed to tourism as a development priority, is more investor-friendly than at any previous point in Nepal’s history.

The registration process is complex. Ten steps across five government authorities, a multi-year construction timeline, and a demanding physical classification standard that requires careful project design from the very beginning. But the complexity is front-loaded. Once the hotel is classified and operational, the ongoing compliance obligations are manageable, the regulatory environment is predictable, and the business opportunity is real.

The investors who succeed in Nepal’s hotel sector are those who invest in thorough pre-investment preparation, the feasibility study, the legal due diligence, the classification standard review, and the regulatory mapping, before breaking ground. The investors who struggle are those who discover after construction that their building doesn’t meet the classification standards, or that they missed the NRB recording deadline and can’t repatriate their profits.

If you are considering a hotel investment in Nepal, we would be glad to help you navigate the path from concept to classification.

“NPR 350 billion has already been invested in Nepal’s hotel industry. The investors who built those hotels understood one thing clearly: the regulatory process is demanding, but the destination is worth it. Nepal’s mountains will still be there in fifty years. The question is whether your hotel will be part of the story.”

title: Establishing an Industry in Nepal as a Foreigner: FITTA 2019 Guide
content:
Establishing an industry as a foreigner is one of the more involved routes into Nepal, and one of the most rewarding when it is done properly. The country wants manufacturing and industrial investment, and the legal framework reflects that. What the framework also reflects, with equal clarity, is that industrial activity touches land, environment, labour and foreign exchange all at once, and each of those sits with a different authority.

This guide explains the full route in plain language, from the first approval to the day your plant is operating, so you can plan with realistic expectations rather than guesswork.

Quick answer

This guide covers everything a foreigner needs to know about establishing an industry in Nepal in 2025, including the full legal framework (FITTA 2019, FITTR 2021, IEA 2020, Companies Act 2063), the nine forms of foreign investment under FITTA Section 2(j), who qualifies as a foreign investor (including Non-Resident Nepalis and venture capital funds from January 2025), the FITTA Negative List of prohibited sectors, the IEA industry classification by capital size (micro to large) and type (manufacturing/service/infrastructure), the two-route system (Automatic Route: 7 working days for investments up to NPR 500 million vs Standard Route for larger projects), the complete 10-step registration process from OSSC FDI application through NRB investment recording, the FITTR 2021 three-stage investment injection schedule under Rule 9, the full 14-document checklist, government fees and realistic timelines (2-3 months total), foreign equity caps by sector, comprehensive tax incentives (including complete income tax exemption for mountain region industries, SEZ benefits), investor protections under FITTA (nationalization protection, international arbitration, 15-day repatriation guarantee), profit repatriation procedure, post-registration compliance obligations, common challenges and how to avoid them, and 12 detailed FAQs. Researched and verified against 2025 regulations including the January 2025 FITTA amendment and FY 2024/25 Automatic Route adoption statistics.

Introduction: Why Nepal Is Attracting More Foreign Industrialists Than Ever

Something has genuinely shifted in Nepal’s investment story. In the first nine months of fiscal year 2024/25, Nepal recorded approximately NPR 58 billion in foreign investment commitments, with a remarkable 97% of those commitments flowing through the Automatic Route that the government introduced in 2023. That single statistic matters: it tells you the reforms are real, the process has meaningfully improved, and foreign investors worldwide are responding.

China contributes 45.34% of Nepal’s total foreign direct investment. India follows at 21.54%. The remaining third comes from Hong Kong, South Korea, the United States, the United Kingdom, Singapore, Spain, Australia, and a growing list of countries discovering what Nepal’s position between the world’s two largest economies actually means for manufacturing, energy, technology, services, and hospitality.

What does 'establishing an industry' mean in Nepal’s legal framework? It means more than opening a consulting office or a retail shop. In Nepal, an 'industry' is a specific category of business as defined by the Industrial Enterprises Act (IEA) 2020, one that produces goods, provides services, or engages in any activity classified as an industrial enterprise under the Act. This classification is the prerequisite for foreign investment: FITTA 2019 is explicit that foreign investment can only be made in businesses that qualify as an industry under the IEA. If your proposed activity does not meet the IEA’s definition, FDI approval cannot be granted.

This guide is written for foreign entrepreneurs evaluating Nepal entry, multinational companies considering a Nepali subsidiary, Non-Resident Nepalis returning to invest, and anyone who needs to understand Nepal’s foreign investment framework in practical, usable detail. It covers every step from eligibility check through to the ongoing compliance obligations that follow your industry’s first day of operations.

“In FY 2024/25, 97% of Nepal’s foreign investment commitments, nearly NPR 58 billion, came through the Automatic Route. The reforms are working. Nepal is open for business in ways it simply was not five years ago. The question is whether your preparation matches the opportunity.”

The Legal Framework: Laws That Govern Foreign Industry Establishment in Nepal

Nepal’s foreign investment framework is built on four primary laws that work together. Understanding how they interact is not academic, it directly determines which approval route you use, which authority you approach first, and what documents you need.

Law

Year

What It Governs for Foreign Investors

Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA)

2019 (2076 BS)

The cornerstone legislation. Defines foreign investment in nine distinct forms, eligible sectors, minimum thresholds, the Automatic and Standard approval routes, investor protections (national treatment, repatriation guarantee, dispute resolution), profit repatriation rules, and technology transfer provisions. Amended January 2025 to allow investment through venture capital funds registered with SEBON.

Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Regulations (FITTR)

2021 (2077 BS)

Implements FITTA procedurally. Provides document requirements, the critical 3-stage investment injection schedule under Rule 9, timelines for each stage, royalty payment limits for technology transfer agreements (capped at 5% of net annual sales), and operational guidance for the Automatic Route.

Industrial Enterprises Act (IEA)

2020 (2076 BS)

Defines what constitutes an 'industry' eligible for foreign investment. Classifies industries by fixed asset size (micro/cottage/small/medium/large) and by type (manufacturing/service/infrastructure/agro-processing/energy/mining). Foreign investment can ONLY be made in businesses that qualify as industries under this Act. Also provides the tax incentive framework by industry category and location.

Companies Act (Kampani Ain)

2063 (2006)

Governs company incorporation at the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR). All foreign-invested industries must be incorporated as Private Limited or Public Limited companies. Company registration follows FDI approval and precedes industry registration. The CAMIS portal (camis.ocr.gov.np) is the online interface.

Income Tax Act

2058 (2002)

Corporate income tax at 25% standard rate. Specific reduced rates and multi-year full exemptions for certain industry types and geographic locations. PAN registration mandatory before any commercial operations.

Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA)

2019 BS (1962)

All FDI capital must enter Nepal through official banking channels (SWIFT). No cash investments permitted. Each foreign currency injection must be recorded with Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) within 6 months of receipt. Governs profit repatriation.

Special Economic Zone Act

2073 (2016)

Governs investment in Nepal’s SEZs (Bhairahawa, Simara, and others). Investors in SEZs receive enhanced incentives: 10-year full income tax exemption, duty-free import of raw materials, and dividend tax exemption for first 5 years. Key destination for export-oriented manufacturers.

⚖️ The One Stop Service Centre (OSSC): The OSSC at the Department of Industry (DoI), Tripureshwor, Kathmandu, is the primary interface for all FDI registration activities. It brings together the DoI, OCR, IRD, NRB, Department of Immigration, and other agencies under one roof. Online portal: imis.doind.gov.np. Office hours: Sunday, Friday, 10:00 AM, 5:00 PM. For investments above NPR 6 billion, approach the Investment Board Nepal (IBN) at Singha Durbar instead.

Who Qualifies as a Foreign Investor Under Nepal’s Law?

The definition of 'foreign investor' under FITTA 2019 Section 2(h) is deliberately broad. It encompasses far more than just passport-holding foreigners.

Investor Type

Definition Under FITTA 2019

Key Notes

Foreign individual

Any person who is not a Nepali citizen

Includes foreign nationals of any country with which Nepal has diplomatic relations

Foreign company / firm

Any company or business entity incorporated outside Nepal

Can be 100% foreign-owned. Must provide authenticated corporate documents.

Non-Resident Nepali (NRN)

Nepali citizen permanently residing abroad with NRN status

Classified as foreign investor but with some preferential provisions. Can invest in some sectors restricted to other foreigners.

Foreign government / agency

Sovereign wealth funds, development finance institutions, international agencies

Subject to specific sector restrictions based on Nepal’s bilateral agreements.

Institutional foreign investor

Foreign investment funds, private equity firms, venture capital funds

From January 2025: venture capital funds registered with SEBON in Nepal can be used as FDI vehicles (new FITTA amendment).

✅ Non-Resident Nepali Advantage: If you hold NRN status, confirm it through the Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) before applying. NRNs can invest in certain sectors restricted to purely foreign nationals and may access preferential investment pathways under the NRN Act.

Nine Forms of Foreign Investment Recognised Under FITTA 2019

Section 2(j) of FITTA 2019 defines foreign investment to include nine distinct forms. The form your investment takes affects the approval process, NRB recording requirements, and applicable repatriation rules. Understanding this from the outset shapes your investment structure correctly.

Investment Form

Description

Key Considerations

Equity investment (shares)

Subscription or purchase of shares in a Nepali company

Most common form. Subject to the FITTR Rule 9 three-stage injection schedule. Ownership proportional to share percentage.

Convertible bonds / debentures

Investment through bonds convertible into equity shares

Subject to SEBON regulations. Useful for staged entry where investor wants debt-like instrument initially.

Loans from foreign financial institutions

Project loans from foreign banks or financial institutions

Requires Ministry of Industry recommendation + NRB approval. Cannot be from parent company, must be from a financial institution per FITTA Section 12.

Technology transfer

Contribution of proprietary technology, know-how, patents, or brand licences in exchange for equity or royalties

Royalties capped at 5% of net annual sales under FITTR. TTA must be registered with DoI. Subject to NRB approval for royalty remittance.

Lease investment

Investment through leasing of aircraft, ships, machinery, construction equipment

Introduced by FITTA 2019 (not in previous law). Useful for capital-intensive industries needing equipment without purchase capital.

Reinvestment of earnings

Reinvesting dividends or profits generated in Nepal back into the company

Treated as additional FDI. Counts toward approved investment schedule. Reduces need for further foreign currency injection.

Venture capital funds

Investment through VC funds or specialized investment funds registered with SEBON

Introduced by January 2025 FITTA amendment. Opens institutional investment pathways not previously available.

Merger and acquisition

Acquisition of shares or assets of an existing Nepali company

Requires FDI approval even for acquisitions of existing companies. Must respect foreign equity caps where they apply.

Other approved forms

Any other form approved by DoI or IBN

Requires specific regulatory approval and is assessed case by case.

What Industries Can Foreigners Invest In? The Open Sectors and the Negative List

FITTA 2019 uses a negative list approach: all sectors are open for foreign investment EXCEPT those specifically listed in the FITTA Schedule as prohibited or restricted. The March 2025 FITTA amendment further expanded the open sectors by removing the previous positive-list requirement from the Industrial Enterprises Act. This is a significantly more investor-friendly framework than what existed before 2019.

5.1 Prohibited and Restricted Sectors (The Negative List)

⚠️ These Sectors Cannot Accept Foreign Investment: Investing in any Negative List sector results in FDI approval denial. Attempting to circumvent these restrictions through nominee arrangements or mislabelled business activities constitutes fraud and carries criminal liability under Nepal’s laws.

5.2 Priority Sectors Where Nepal Actively Encourages Foreign Investment

  • Hydropower and renewable energy generation, Nepal’s greatest export potential
  • Manufacturing (especially export-oriented), currently Nepal’s smallest FDI sector by commitment, with enormous growth room
  • Information technology and software development, no minimum investment threshold
  • Tourism and hospitality, hotels, resorts (NOT travel/trekking agencies)
  • Healthcare and medical services
  • Education institutions
  • Infrastructure, roads, bridges, airports, tunnels
  • Mining and mineral processing
  • Pharmaceuticals and medical devices
  • Agro-processing and food manufacturing (not primary farming)
  • Special Economic Zones, enhanced incentives for all qualifying industries

IEA 2020 Industry Classification: Where Does Your Business Fit?

Before approaching any government office, identify how the IEA 2020 classifies your business. This determines which regulatory authority handles your file, what tax incentives apply, and what operational obligations you will carry.

6.1 Classification by Fixed Assets (Capital Size)

📌 Minimum FDI vs Industry Category: The NPR 20 million minimum FDI threshold places most foreign-invested businesses squarely in the Medium or Large category administered by the DoI. Micro, cottage, and small industries with fixed assets below NPR 5 million are generally inaccessible to foreign investors because they fall below the FITTA minimum threshold.

6.2 Classification by Business Type

Industry Type

Examples Relevant to Foreign Investors

Manufacturing

Food processing, garments, pharmaceuticals, electronics assembly, cement, steel, chemicals, packaging

The Two Approval Routes: Automatic vs Standard

Nepal’s 2023 Automatic Route was the most transformative single reform in the country’s FDI history. The 97% adoption rate in FY 2024/25 tells you everything about how foreign investors have responded. Here is what each route means in practice.

Factor

Automatic Route

Standard Route

Investment size

Up to NPR 500 million (~USD 3.8 million)

Approval authority

Department of Industry (DoI), FITT Unit at OSSC

FY 2024/25 adoption

Best suited for

Large infrastructure, power, mega projects

✔ 97% Chose Automatic: In FY 2024/25, approximately 97% of Nepal’s foreign investment commitments, nearly NPR 58 billion, came through the Automatic Route. This is the normal pathway for the vast majority of foreign investors.

The Complete 10-Step Process: How to Establish an Industry in Nepal as a Foreigner

The registration process for a foreign-invested industry in Nepal involves 10 sequential steps across multiple government agencies. Each step’s output is a mandatory input for the next. The OSSC at Tripureshwor coordinates many of these steps under one roof, which is a significant practical improvement over the pre-2023 multi-office process.

STEP 1 Sector Eligibility Check and Investment Structure Decision

Before approaching any government office, answer two questions with certainty:

  • Is your sector open? Confirm that your proposed industry is not on the FITTA Negative List. The DoI’s website (doind.gov.np) publishes the current list. For any uncertainty, get a written legal opinion from a Nepal-based FDI lawyer before committing capital.
  • Does your business qualify as an IEA industry? Foreign investment can ONLY be made in businesses classified as industries under the IEA 2020. Confirm this classification before proceeding.

Also decide your ownership structure:

  • 100% wholly foreign-owned company (permitted in most open sectors)
  • Joint venture with Nepali partner (not legally required except in equity-capped sectors, but often strategically valuable)
  • Acquisition of existing Nepali company shares (requires FDI approval for the acquisition itself)
  • Technology transfer combined with equity investment

✅ Invest in a Legal Opinion First: A sector eligibility assessment and investment structure opinion from a qualified Nepal FDI lawyer costs a fraction of the cost of a rejected application or misdirected structure. It is the most cost-effective preparation step available.

ℹ️ Timeline: 1-2 weeks for legal opinion and structure decision.

STEP 2 Prepare the Investment Proposal and Authenticate Documents

The FDI approval application requires a comprehensive, consistent package of documents. Completeness at the time of first submission is critical, especially for Automatic Route applications where the 7-day statutory clock begins at receipt of a COMPLETE application. Incomplete applications trigger queries that pause the clock and delay approval.

Complete document checklist for FDI approval:

  1. Prescribed FDI application form (from the OSSC at imis.doind.gov.np or in person)
  2. Project proposal / feasibility study: business description, market analysis, investment amount and source, employment projections, technology details if any, environmental considerations
  3. Bio-data (personal details form) of the foreign investor: full name, address, nationality, occupation, date of birth, contact details
  4. Copy of the foreign investor’s valid passport (all biographical pages)
  5. Certificate of Incorporation of the foreign investing company (if investor is a company), with apostille or Nepal Embassy authentication
  6. Memorandum of Association (MOA) and Articles of Association (AOA) of the foreign investing company, apostilled/authenticated + certified English or Nepali translation
  7. Financial Credibility Certificate (FCC): A letter from the foreign investor’s home-country commercial bank confirming financial standing and capacity to make the proposed investment. Must be recent (within 6 months of application)
  8. Board Resolution of the foreign investing company authorizing the Nepal investment and designating the authorized representative (if investor is a company)
  9. Joint Venture Agreement (if investing with a Nepali partner), notarized
  10. Citizenship certificate of any Nepali partner/shareholder
  11. Power of attorney (if filing through a Nepal-based agent or legal representative)
  12. Source of funds declaration and documentary support
  13. Draft Technology Transfer Agreement (if the investment involves technology contribution)
  14. Application fee payment proof

⚠️ Authentication Takes Time: Foreign company documents (Certificate of Incorporation, MOA, Board Resolution) must be apostilled (if the home country is a Hague Convention member) or authenticated by the Nepal Embassy in the home country. Allow 1-3 weeks for this process, and start it before everything else.

ℹ️ Timeline: Document preparation and authentication: 2-4 weeks (authentication often takes longest).

STEP 3 Submit FDI Application at the OSSC (Department of Industry)

Submit the complete application package to the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer (FITT) Unit at the One Stop Service Centre (OSSC), Department of Industry, Tripureshwor, Kathmandu. For Automatic Route investments, you can also submit online at imis.doind.gov.np.

OSSC officers conduct a preliminary completeness review. If documents are complete and consistent:

  • Automatic Route (up to NPR 500M): DoI issues the FDI Approval Certificate within 7 working days under FITTA Section 15(2). No additional ministry consultations required.
  • Standard Route (NPR 500M, 6B): DoI conducts a detailed review, which may include consultation with sector-specific ministries. Timeline: 30-45 working days.
  • Investment Board Nepal (above NPR 6B): IBN conducts its own comprehensive project review. Timeline: 60-90 days. Involves higher-level government engagement for major projects.

The FDI Approval Certificate specifies the approved investment amount, business sector, shareholding structure, and the investment injection schedule. It is the foundational authorization document for all subsequent steps.

✔ FDI Approved! The DoI FDI Approval Certificate is the most important document you will receive in this entire process. Keep multiple certified copies. Every subsequent registration step requires it.

ℹ️ Timeline: Automatic Route: 7 working days. Standard Route: 30-45 working days.

STEP 4 Register the Company at the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR)

With the FDI Approval Certificate in hand, incorporate the Nepali company through the CAMIS portal at camis.ocr.gov.np. The FDI Approval Certificate is a mandatory prerequisite, the OCR will not register a company with foreign shareholders without it.

Company Structure Options

  • Private Limited Company (Pvt. Ltd.), recommended for most FDI: Minimum 1 shareholder, maximum 101 shareholders. Most flexible governance. Standard for small to medium investments.
  • Public Limited Company: Minimum 7 promoters. Required for industries planning to raise capital from the public or eventually list on NEPSE. Appropriate for large-scale infrastructure or manufacturing projects.

Critical MOA Requirement

The company’s Memorandum of Association MUST clearly state the industry type and business activities as approved in the FDI Approval Certificate. Any discrepancy between the MOA business objectives and the FDI-approved activities creates problems at the industry registration stage and during DoI monitoring visits. The MOA must be drafted with the FDI Approval Certificate in hand, not before it.

Additional documents required for OCR registration:

  1. DoI FDI Approval Certificate (mandatory prerequisite)
  2. Completed CAMIS portal application
  3. MOA, business objectives matching approved FDI activities exactly
  4. Articles of Association (AOA), internal governance rules
  5. Passport copies of foreign shareholders (apostilled/authenticated)
  6. Citizenship certificates of any Nepali shareholders
  7. Photographs of all shareholders and directors
  8. Proposed registered office address documentation
  9. Digital Signature Certificate (DSC), required for authenticated CAMIS submission
  10. OCR registration fee payment

ℹ️ Timeline: OCR company registration: 7-10 working days from complete submission.

STEP 5 PAN and VAT Registration at the Inland Revenue Department (IRD)

Every company in Nepal, including foreign-invested industries, must register for a Permanent Account Number (PAN) at the IRD before commencing any commercial activity. PAN is your company’s tax identity and is required for opening a bank account, issuing invoices, signing contracts, and filing tax returns.

VAT registration is mandatory if projected annual turnover exceeds NPR 50 lakhs for goods businesses or NPR 30 lakhs for service businesses. For most medium and large industries, VAT registration is standard practice from the outset.

The IRD’s online PAN/VAT registration at ird.gov.np is straightforward with the OCR Registration Certificate and FDI Approval Certificate as primary supporting documents.

ℹ️ Timeline: PAN and VAT registration: 3-5 working days.

STEP 6 Ward Office Registration and Business Operation Permit

Register with the Ward Office (Wada Karyalaya) of the local municipality where the industry’s premises will be physically located. This local government authorization, the Business Operation Permit (Sanchalana Anumati Patra), is specifically required for physical operation of the business at that address. It is separate from all central government approvals and must be renewed annually.

Submit: OCR Registration Certificate, PAN certificate, and lease or ownership documentation for the business premises. The Ward Office may inspect the premises before issuing the permit.

ℹ️ Timeline: Ward Office registration: 3-7 working days.

STEP 7 Industry Registration at the Department of Industry (DoI)

This is the step most foreign investors overlook. OCR registration makes your company a legal entity. Industry registration at the DoI makes it a registered industry eligible for industrial incentives, entitled to operate as an industrial enterprise, and subject to the one-year commencement obligation.

The Industry Registration Certificate issued by the DoI establishes your industry’s official category (medium/large), determines eligibility for sector-specific tax incentives, and starts the one-year clock for commencement of operations.

Documents to submit to the DoI Industry Registration Section:

  1. DoI FDI Approval Certificate
  2. OCR Company Registration Certificate
  3. MOA and AOA
  4. PAN certificate
  5. Ward Office Business Operation Permit
  6. Business premises documentation (lease agreement or ownership proof)
  7. Project plan and employment projections

⚠️ One-Year Commencement Obligation: From the date the Industry Registration Certificate is issued, the industry has ONE YEAR to commence commercial operations. For construction-phase industries: active, documented construction activity satisfies this requirement. For service industries: generating first commercial revenue. Failure to commence within one year can result in cancellation of the Industry Registration Certificate and complications with the FDI approval.

ℹ️ Timeline: Industry registration at DoI: 7-10 working days.

STEP 8 Open Corporate Bank Account and Inject Foreign Investment Capital

Open a corporate bank account at any commercial bank in Nepal in the company’s name. Then remit the foreign investment capital from your home country through official banking channels (SWIFT transfer) directly into this account. Cash investments are not permitted under Nepal’s FERA.

The Three-Stage Investment Injection Schedule (FITTR 2021 Rule 9)

Rule 9 of the FITTR 2021 mandates a phased capital injection schedule. This is one of the most misunderstood compliance requirements for foreign investors in Nepal:

Stage

Minimum Injection Required

Deadline from FDI Approval Date

Stage 1 (for investments of NPR 50M+)

At least 25% of the total approved investment amount

Within 1 year of FDI Approval Certificate date

Stage 2

Within 3 years of FDI Approval Certificate date

The bank issues an Investment Inflow Certificate upon receipt of each foreign currency remittance. Retain this document carefully, it is a mandatory submission for the NRB recording step that follows.

📌 In-Kind Investment: Foreign investment through machinery, equipment, and technology (in-kind) is permitted under FITTA. In-kind investment requires prior DoI approval for asset valuation by an approved certified valuator before import into Nepal.

ℹ️ Timeline: Bank account opening: 3-7 working days. SWIFT transfers: 3-5 business days per transaction.

STEP 9 Record the Investment with Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB)

This is the step that determines whether you can ever get your money back out of Nepal. Within 6 months of each foreign currency injection into your Nepali bank account, the company must formally record the investment with Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB). Without this recording:

  • Future dividends and profits cannot be repatriated through official channels
  • The original investment capital cannot be returned to the investor
  • Technology transfer royalties cannot be remitted abroad
  • Capital gains from share sales cannot be repatriated

Submit to NRB at Baluwatar, Kathmandu:

  1. Investment Inflow Certificate from the commercial bank confirming each foreign currency receipt
  2. Share Registry Certificate (Sher Darta Pramaanpatra) from OCR confirming shareholding
  3. DoI FDI Approval Certificate
  4. OCR Company Registration Certificate
  5. PAN certificate

NRB issues the Investment Recording Certificate (also called the NRB Investment Certificate). Keep this permanently, it is required for every future repatriation application.

⚠️ 6-Month Deadline Is Non-Negotiable: FITTA regulations require NRB recording within 6 months of each capital injection. This is not a soft guideline. Set a calendar reminder from the date each SWIFT transfer is received by your Nepali bank. Missing this deadline creates regulatory complications that require additional NRB review to resolve, which can take months.

ℹ️ Timeline: NRB recording: 2-3 weeks from complete document submission.

STEP 10 Obtain Sector-Specific Licenses and Commence Operations

Depending on your industry type, additional sector-specific licenses or approvals are required before commencing commercial operations. These are mandatory, operating without them in regulated sectors carries criminal liability, not just administrative penalties.

Tax Incentives and Investor Benefits: What Nepal Offers

Nepal’s government offers a substantial package of fiscal incentives designed to attract quality foreign investment in priority sectors and underdeveloped regions. These incentives are not trivial, a manufacturing industry in a mountain district can operate completely tax-free for 10 years.

The 10-year full income tax exemption, combined with duty-free raw material imports and dividend tax exemptions, makes SEZ investment significantly more financially attractive than non-SEZ locations for industries whose products can be exported.

Profit Repatriation: How to Get Your Returns Out of Nepal

The right to repatriate profits is guaranteed by FITTA 2019 and is one of the most investor-friendly provisions in Nepal’s legal framework. For investors who have maintained proper NRB recording from day one, the process is well-defined and predictable.

11.1 What Can Be Repatriated

  • Dividends: Net dividends after payment of the 15% dividend withholding tax on amounts paid to foreign shareholders.
  • Operating profits: Net profits after payment of applicable corporate income tax.
  • Capital gains: Gains from sale of shares, after applicable capital gains tax (which varies based on holding period).
  • Technology transfer royalties: Royalties under registered Technology Transfer Agreements, capped at 5% of net annual sales. NRB must approve the underlying TTA before royalties can be remitted.
  • Return of principal investment: Original invested capital, subject to a general expectation that investors should not repatriate principal within 1 year of injection. After 1 year, NRB approval is required.

11.2 Step-by-Step Repatriation Process

  1. Obtain a current Tax Clearance Certificate from the Inland Revenue Department confirming all Nepal taxes are fully paid
  2. Pass a Board Resolution approving the dividend distribution or other repatriation, with proper corporate governance documentation
  3. Apply to Nepal Rastra Bank with the NRB Investment Recording Certificate, audited financial statements, Board Resolution, tax clearance certificate, and the repatriation application form
  4. NRB must respond within 15 days of a complete application under FITTA Section 20, this is a statutory guarantee
  5. Upon NRB approval, the company’s commercial bank executes the SWIFT transfer to the investor’s designated foreign bank account

📌 15-Day Guarantee: FITTA Section 20 requires NRB to grant repatriation permission within 15 days of a complete application. This statutory timeframe makes Nepal’s profit repatriation process significantly more predictable than many comparable South Asian jurisdictions.

Establishing the industry is the beginning of your regulatory relationship with Nepal’s government, not the end. Foreign-invested industries carry a comprehensive set of ongoing compliance obligations. The most critical, the NRB recording deadline and the commencement obligation, have been emphasised throughout this guide because they are the most commonly missed.
