title: Trademark Registration in Nepal: A Practical Guide for Businesses
content:
A brand is often worth more than the premises it is sold from, yet plenty of businesses in Nepal trade for years without ever registering their name. Nothing goes wrong until it does: a copycat opens nearby, a former partner launches under a similar mark, or an online listing uses your name to draw your customers. Registration is what turns a name you use into a right you can enforce.

This guide explains how trademark registration works in Nepal and why the timing of your filing matters.

Quick answer

Trademarks in Nepal are registered with the Department of Industry under the Patent, Design and Trademark Act, 2022. Registration grants a statutory monopoly over the mark and a clear basis to act against counterfeiters and copycats. The process runs from a preliminary search, through examination, to publication and registration. A registered mark is valid for seven years and can be renewed.

Where you file

The Department of Industry administers patents, industrial designs and trademarks from its office in Kathmandu. Because one office handles all three, the system is centralised, which makes the filing route predictable. The trade-off is that a busy office rewards a well-prepared application over a rushed one.

The registration process

  1. Preliminary search. Check for conflicting marks already on the register before you commit to a name or a filing.
  2. File the application. Include a representation of the mark and the applicant's details.
  3. Examination. The Department of Industry examines the mark for distinctiveness and conflicts.
  4. Publication. The mark is published, opening a window for opposition.
  5. Registration. If no opposition succeeds, the mark is registered.

Why distinctiveness matters

A mark must be capable of distinguishing your goods or services from those of others. Descriptive words, common surnames and generic terms are frequently rejected, unless they have acquired a distinct meaning through long use. A name that describes exactly what you sell is easy to market and hard to protect. A name that is distinctive may need a little more explanation, but it is the one that can be defended.

Duration and renewal

A registered trademark is initially valid for seven years and can be renewed for successive periods. Renewal is a simple filing, but missing the deadline can remove the mark from the register, and rebuilding protection after a lapse is far harder than keeping it alive.

A worked example

Two cafes open in the same district within a year of each other, both called something close to a well-known coffee brand. Neither registered. When the original brand owner enters Nepal, both are served notice. The owner who filed a trademark application early is in a strong position to oppose the copy or to license the mark. The owner who relied on the common law of passing off must prove reputation and confusion, which is slower and more expensive, and the outcome is less certain. The cost of the filing, paid early, is trivial next to the cost of the dispute.

Enforcing your rights

A registered proprietor can oppose conflicting applications, demand that infringing use stop, and pursue civil remedies or criminal action. An unregistered mark can only rely on passing off, which requires proving goodwill and misrepresentation and is both harder and costlier. Registration does not remove the need to police a mark, but it changes the odds decisively in your favour.

Frequently asked questions

How long does trademark registration take in Nepal? It varies with examination and any opposition, but the process is predictable once the application is filed. A search before filing avoids the most common delay.

How long is a trademark valid? Seven years initially, renewable for successive periods.

Can I register a descriptive name? Usually not, unless it has acquired a distinct meaning through use.

What can I do if someone copies my mark? If registered, you can oppose their application and act against their use. If unregistered, you depend on passing off, which is harder to prove.

Do I need the mark registered before I use it? You can use a mark before registering it, but you gain enforceable rights only on registration.

Does a foreign trademark cover me in Nepal? No. Protection is territorial, so a mark registered abroad does not protect you in Nepal.

title: Renewable Energy Projects in Nepal: Legal and Regulatory Overview
content:
Nepal's rivers have powered the country for generations, and they remain the centre of its energy ambitions. A hydropower project is also one of the most heavily regulated investments anyone can make here, not because the law is hostile, but because a river is a shared resource and a large dam touches land, forests, communities and the national grid at once. Developers who understand the licensing chain early move faster than those who learn it by trial.

This guide gives an overview of the legal and regulatory framework for renewable energy projects in Nepal, with a focus on hydropower.

Quick answer

Renewable energy projects in Nepal are governed mainly by the Electricity Act, 2049 and the Electricity Regulations, 2050, with larger priority projects falling under the Investment Board Act. A developer needs a survey licence, then a generation licence, plus environmental approval. Power is normally sold to the Nepal Electricity Authority under a power purchase agreement. Foreign investment adds approval and repatriation requirements.

The primary legislation

The Electricity Act, 2049 and the Electricity Regulations, 2050 govern the generation, transmission and distribution of electricity. The Investment Board Act applies to projects that fall within the national priority thresholds and are handled by the Investment Board Nepal. Alongside these sit environmental law, land and forest rules, and, for foreign investors, FITTA and Nepal Rastra Bank's foreign exchange framework.

Licensing requirements

A project typically needs these in sequence:

  • A survey licence to carry out studies and feasibility assessments.
  • An electricity generation licence once the survey and studies are complete.
  • Approval of an environmental impact assessment (EIA), or an initial environmental examination (IEE) for smaller projects.

Each stage depends on the one before it, which is why a project can be delayed substantially by an incomplete study or an environmental file that is submitted too early.

Power purchase agreements

The Nepal Electricity Authority is the principal off-taker. The terms of the power purchase agreement, including tariffs and take-or-pay obligations, are negotiated against the prevailing regulatory framework and often decide whether a project is bankable. Because the PPA sits at the centre of project revenue, its negotiation deserves as much care as the technical design.

Project finance

Lenders typically require a complete chain of land rights, generation and transmission licences, a signed PPA, and adequate insurance before they will commit. Foreign investors should confirm whether their project needs Investment Board Nepal approval or a sectoral licence. Most financing delays trace back to a gap in the licence chain rather than to the money itself.

Environmental and social compliance

Hydropower and renewable projects face close environmental and social scrutiny. Resettlement, forest clearance and river-flow obligations must be addressed in the EIA and monitored through the life of the project. These are not only legal requirements. They are also, increasingly, what a project's lenders and off-takers expect to see properly handled.

A worked example

A foreign developer identifies a run-of-river site and secures a survey licence. The feasibility study is thorough, and the land rights chain is assembled before the environmental file is finalised, so the generation licence and EIA approval are not held up by a missing link. The PPA is negotiated with a clear tariff and take-or-pay terms, and the lenders are satisfied. A second developer moves faster and applies for the generation licence before land rights are settled. The file stalls for months, the PPA window narrows, and the financing costs rise. The technical projects are similar. The disciplined sequence is what separates them.

Frequently asked questions

What licences does a hydropower project need? A survey licence, an electricity generation licence, and environmental approval, in sequence.

Who buys the electricity? The Nepal Electricity Authority is the principal off-taker, under a power purchase agreement.

Is environmental approval always required? Yes, in some form. Larger projects need a full EIA, while smaller projects may qualify for an IEE.

Do foreign investors need separate approval? Often yes, especially for larger projects under the Investment Board Nepal, and always under FITTA for the foreign investment itself.

What do lenders require? A complete land rights chain, the relevant licences, a signed PPA, and adequate insurance.

How long does licensing take? It varies widely with project size and the completeness of the studies and environmental file. The sequence, not the calendar, is the main variable.

title: Employment Law in Nepal: Employee Rights and Employer Obligations
content:
Hiring your first employee in Nepal feels simple until the paperwork arrives. The Labour Act sets minimum standards that apply whether or not an employer has thought about them, and the obligations mostly fall on the employer by default. A business that treats employment as a handshake tends to discover the rules only when a dispute or an inspection forces the question.

This guide explains the main employer obligations under the Labour Act, 2074, and how to stay compliant without overcomplicating the basics.

Quick answer

The Labour Act, 2074 governs employment in Nepal and applies to most private sector employers. It prescribes minimum standards for written contracts, working hours, leave, termination and social security. Employers must issue written contracts, keep proper records, contribute to the Social Security Fund, and follow the statutory procedure before terminating employment.

Written employment contracts

An employer must provide a written contract or appointment letter to every employee. The document should set out the nature of the work, the remuneration, the working hours, and the grounds and procedure for termination. A clear contract protects both sides, and it is the first thing a labour office will ask to see if there is a complaint.

Working hours and leave

The standard working week is limited to 48 hours, with overtime payable for additional work. Employees are entitled to annual leave, sick leave and public holidays, along with maternity and paternity leave as prescribed by the statute. These are minimums, not suggestions, and they cannot be traded away in a contract.

Termination and severance

Termination must follow the procedure in the Labour Act. An employee whose services are terminated, other than for misconduct, is entitled to notice or pay in lieu, and to gratuity and leave encashment where applicable. The procedural steps matter as much as the money: a termination that is fair in substance but wrong in process can still be found unlawful.

Social security

Registered employers must contribute to the Social Security Fund on behalf of their employees. Contributions cover medical, accident, dependency and pension benefits, and late or non-payment attracts penalties. Enrolling new staff promptly, rather than in a batch at year end, avoids both the penalty and the administrative scramble.

Practical compliance steps

  • Maintain attendance records, payroll documentation and statutory registers.
  • Issue written contracts and keep signed copies on file.
  • Enrol employees in the Social Security Fund on time.
  • Ensure workplace policies meet anti-discrimination and occupational safety obligations.
  • Follow the statutory process before any termination.

A worked example

A growing marketing firm hires eight staff in a year and, being busy, issues offer letters that omit the termination procedure and working hours. When one employee's performance fails to improve, the firm dismisses him with immediate effect. The dismissal is overturned as procedurally flawed, and the firm pays compensation it could have avoided. A one-page contract drafted at the start, with the statutory procedure spelled out, would have made the same decision defensible. The lesson is common to most labour disputes: the paperwork you disliked at the beginning is the paperwork that protects you at the end.

Frequently asked questions

Is a written contract required? Yes. Employers must provide a written contract or appointment letter to every employee.

What is the maximum working week? 48 hours, with overtime payable beyond that.

What is an employee entitled to on termination? Notice or pay in lieu, and gratuity and leave encashment where applicable, unless the termination is for misconduct.

title: Divorce in Nepal: Process, Cost and Timeline Explained
content:
Deciding to end a marriage is rarely a single moment. For most people it follows a long period of trying to make things work, and by the time they speak to a lawyer they are carrying both the emotional weight of the decision and a set of practical fears about money, children and paperwork. The law in Nepal is clearer than many expect, but it moves along two very different tracks, and knowing which one you are on early makes the whole process easier to bear.

This guide explains both tracks, what each involves, and how to prepare, so you can make decisions calmly rather than under pressure.

Quick answer

There are two routes to divorce in Nepal. A mutual consent divorce, under Section 93 of the Muluki Civil Code, 2074, is when both spouses agree to end the marriage and settle the terms. A contested divorce, based on a recognised ground, is when one spouse does not agree or the terms cannot be settled. Mutual cases are faster and cheaper. Contested cases take longer, because the court must decide custody, maintenance and property along the way.

The law behind it

Divorce in Nepal is governed by Chapter 3 of the National Civil Code, 2074 (the Muluki Civil Code), and by the National Civil Procedure Code for the process itself. The case is filed in the Family Court, or in the District Court with jurisdiction over the respondent's locality. Because the route and the outcome both turn on the facts, the advice worth having is advice about your facts, not about divorce in the abstract.

Grounds for divorce

Under Section 94, either spouse may petition on grounds such as adultery, desertion, physical or mental cruelty, or having lived apart for three or more consecutive years. Section 95 gives a wife additional grounds, including polygamy by the husband and marital rape. If your situation does not fall neatly into one of these, a mutual consent filing may be the more honest route.

How a mutual consent divorce works

Both spouses file a joint petition and agree the terms. Where children, maintenance or property are involved, those terms should be written into the petition so they are settled, not left for a later dispute. In practice this is the route most couples choose when the relationship has ended without open conflict, because it closes the matter in weeks rather than years. The court can decree the divorce after the prescribed period, which is designed to give both parties time to reconsider.

How a contested divorce works

When only one spouse wants the divorce, or the two cannot agree, the petition must state a recognised ground and the case proceeds through hearings, evidence and, frequently, reconciliation attempts. The court will decide custody, maintenance and how jointly acquired property is divided. Because these decisions are discretionary, the quality of the evidence prepared at the start often decides the outcome more than anything said in the final hearing.

How long it takes

Route Typical timeframe
Mutual consent A few weeks to two to three months after the court accepts the petition
Contested, no major disputes Around one to two years from filing
Contested with custody or property disputes Longer still, and longer again if the respondent cannot be traced

These are realistic ranges, not promises. Court load and the cooperation of both parties move the timeline more than anything else.

Documents you will normally need

  • Citizenship certificates of both spouses
  • The marriage registration certificate, or court marriage certificate
  • Birth certificates for any children
  • Evidence supporting any claim over property or maintenance
  • A properly authenticated power of attorney if a spouse lives abroad

What it costs

The court fee on a divorce plaint in a district court is modest, often a few hundred rupees. The larger cost is professional fees, which depend on whether the matter is mutual or contested and how much negotiation and hearing time it needs. A mutual file can usually be handled on a fixed fee. A contested matter with property and custody issues is typically billed on milestones. Whichever applies, ask for a written fee structure before you engage anyone.

A worked example

A couple who married in Kathmandu and now live in Australia want to divorce by agreement, but neither can easily return. They sign a power of attorney before a notary in Australia, have it attested by the Nepali embassy, and their Nepali lawyer files a mutual consent petition in Kathmandu. The terms on their apartment and on child maintenance are set out in the petition, so there is nothing left to argue about later. The matter is done without either of them flying home. Had one of them opposed the divorce, the same facts would have taken a much longer and more expensive route, and at least one appearance would likely have been required.

Divorce when a spouse lives abroad

Nepali couples living overseas can often complete a mutual consent divorce by power of attorney, avoiding a return to Nepal. Contested cases are harder to run remotely and usually need at least one appearance by the petitioner, or cross-examination of a witness.

Custody, maintenance and property

The court decides custody in the interest of the child, weighing the child's welfare and age against the care each parent can provide. Maintenance reflects the needs of the dependent spouse and children and the ability of the person paying. Property acquired during the marriage through joint effort is generally divided, while ancestral and individually owned property is treated separately. These questions are where most of the emotion in a case sits, and where calm, early advice pays off most.

Practical steps to take

  1. Speak to a family lawyer before filing, so the right route and grounds are chosen.
  2. Gather the documents above, including the original marriage certificate.
  3. If the divorce is mutual, put the terms on custody, maintenance and property in writing first.
  4. File with the correct court and attend the required hearings.
  5. After the decree, update your records and register any new marriage.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a divorce take in Nepal? A mutual consent divorce is typically finalised within a few weeks to two to three months once the court accepts the petition. A contested divorce generally takes one to two years, and longer where custody or property is disputed.

Can I divorce without going to court? No. Even a mutual consent divorce requires a court decree. The agreement shapes the case, but the court issues the order.

Can we divorce in Nepal if we married abroad? Often yes, depending on your citizenship and where the respondent lives. A Nepali couple who married abroad can generally proceed in Nepal, and the marriage may need to be registered here first.

Do I need my spouse's agreement to divorce? No. A contested divorce is available on a recognised ground without the other spouse's consent, though it takes longer.

What happens to property on divorce? Property acquired during the marriage through joint effort is generally divided. Ancestral and individually owned property is treated separately.

Can a spouse abroad be divorced without returning? In mutual cases, usually yes, through an authenticated power of attorney. Contested cases often require an appearance.

title: How to Register an NGO in Nepal: A Step-by-Step Guide
content:
People who set out to do good in Nepal often hit a wall they did not expect, and it is rarely about the cause. It is about paperwork. The registration route for a non-profit depends on whom you intend to serve and where your funding comes from, and choosing the wrong route at the start can stall an organisation before it has done any work at all.

This guide explains the two main routes for non-profits in Nepal, the third path for international organisations, and how to keep a registration in good standing once it is granted.

Quick answer

There are two domestic routes and one international one. A local non-profit registers with the District Administration Office (DAO) if it will work within Nepal under domestic funding. An organisation that operates nationally or receives foreign funding affiliates with the Social Welfare Council (SWC) as well. An International NGO (INGO) enters Nepal under the Social Welfare Act and an agreement with the SWC, and must work through local partners rather than operating directly in the community.

NGO and INGO: what the words mean in practice

In everyday use, an NGO is a domestic non-profit registered with the DAO and affiliated with the Social Welfare Council. An INGO is a foreign non-profit that enters Nepal under the Social Welfare Act and an agreement with the SWC. The distinction matters because an INGO cannot simply run its own projects here. It channels its work through local NGO partners, and its approval process is more regulated.

Step 1: Form the founding committee

You need a group of founding members, usually five or more Nepali citizens, who will form the general assembly and elect an executive committee. Their citizenship certificates, and in most cases passports, are required. Getting the founding group right at this stage saves redoing the documents later.

Step 2: Draft the constitution

The constitution is the heart of the application. It should set out the organisation's name, objectives, area of operation, membership, the composition and tenure of the executive committee, how decisions are taken, and how funds are managed. Supporting documents include the minutes of the formation meeting, the election of office bearers, and the PAN application of the institution. A constitution that is vague about objectives or about how funds are controlled is the most common reason a file is sent back.

Step 3: Register at the District Administration Office

The complete file goes to the DAO of the district where the organisation is based. The DAO reviews the constitution and documents and, once satisfied, issues the registration. This registration gives the organisation legal personality, which it needs before it can open a bank account or sign agreements in its own name.

Step 4: Affiliate with the Social Welfare Council

A registered NGO that intends to receive foreign funding, or to operate beyond the local level, typically registers with and seeks affiliation from the Social Welfare Council. Affiliation is what unlocks access to funding and to formal national recognition. The SWC reviews the constitution, the DAO registration and the organisation's work plan.

Step 5: Bank account and PAN

With the DAO registration and, where applicable, SWC affiliation in hand, the organisation can open a bank account in its own name and complete its tax registration to receive a PAN. These are the prerequisites for receiving funding, issuing receipts and employing staff.

A worked example

A group in Lalitpur wants to run a literacy programme funded entirely by local donors. It follows the DAO route, publishes a clear constitution, and keeps its work within the district. A second group wants to run the same programme but with a European foundation as its funder. That funding brings the Social Welfare Council into the picture, and with it a stricter review of the constitution and work plan. Had the second group registered only with the DAO and then accepted foreign funding, it would have had to pause and restructure mid-programme. Deciding at the outset which route fits your funding is the single most useful early choice.

Ongoing compliance

A non-profit must file annual reports and financial statements with the DAO and, where affiliated, with the Social Welfare Council to keep its registration current. Falling behind on reporting is the most common reason an organisation's status lapses and funding is interrupted. Renewal and reporting dates vary by office, so a compliance calendar from day one is worth the small effort.

Frequently asked questions

How many founding members are needed? Usually five or more Nepali citizens, who form the general assembly and elect the executive committee.

Do I need Social Welfare Council affiliation? If you intend to receive foreign funding or operate beyond the local level, yes. It is central to accessing funding and national recognition.

What is the difference between an NGO and an INGO? An NGO is a domestic non-profit registered with the DAO. An INGO is a foreign non-profit entering Nepal under the Social Welfare Act and working through local partners.

Can an INGO operate directly in Nepal? Generally it must work through local NGO partners rather than operating directly in the community.

Does an NGO need a PAN? Yes. A PAN is required for receiving funding, issuing receipts and employing staff.

What happens if annual reports are missed? The registration and affiliation can lapse, which interrupts funding. Reporting discipline keeps the organisation in good standing.

title: NRN Investment in Nepal: How Non-Resident Nepalis Can Invest
content:
For many non-resident Nepalis, investing back home is both a financial decision and an emotional one. There is a family business to support, or a plot of land to develop, or simply a wish to keep a stake in the country you grew up in. The good news is that NRNs are welcome to invest, and the framework exists. The part that trips people up is the same one that catches every foreign investor: the approvals come before the money, not after.

This guide explains how NRN investment works in Nepal, where the diaspora route differs, and what to get right so your capital is not stranded.

Quick answer

Non-resident Nepalis can invest in Nepal under the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA), which treats NRNs as permitted foreign investors. The usual approvals apply: sector eligibility, approval from the Department of Industry, and registration with the Office of the Company Registrar. In some cases the NRN route carries a lower entry threshold than the general foreign investment minimum, so it is worth confirming the current policy before you structure anything.

Is the NRN route different?

NRNs are foreign investors under FITTA, so the framework is familiar. What differs is treatment. Certain concessions are available to the diaspora, and some technology-based or smaller investments can qualify for a lower threshold than the general minimum. These are policy details that change, which is exactly why they should be checked at the time you invest rather than assumed from something read a year ago.

Ways an NRN can invest

  • A new company in an eligible sector, usually a private limited company with the NRN as shareholder. This is the most common route.
  • Investment in an existing company, by subscribing to new shares, subject to sector limits and the company's approval.
  • Listed securities, meaning portfolio investment in shares on the Nepal Stock Exchange, which follows separate rules for non-residents.
  • A branch or joint venture, where the NRN invests alongside Nepali or other partners.

Minimum investment and sector eligibility

The general minimum foreign investment threshold in Nepal is currently NPR 20 million, and individual sectors carry their own limits or are reserved for Nepali citizens. Energy, tourism, IT and manufacturing are broadly open. Some service and retail activities are reserved. Technology-based investments in certain cases benefit from a lower or waived threshold. Confirm sector eligibility before committing money, because a structure that cannot be approved wastes both the filing cost and months of time.

The process, step by step

  1. Confirm sector eligibility and the minimum investment that applies to an NRN.
  2. Submit the foreign investment application to the Department of Industry and obtain approval.
  3. Reserve the company name and prepare the memorandum and articles of association.
  4. Incorporate at the Office of the Company Registrar and obtain the certificate.
  5. Register for PAN and, where applicable, VAT.
  6. Open a corporate bank account and route the investment through authorised banking channels.

Do you need to be in Nepal?

Much of the process can be handled remotely. A shareholder resolution and a power of attorney can be notarised abroad and authenticated, and a local representative can complete the filings. In practice, being available for one visit at the key banking stage smooths things out, but it is not always essential. Our guide to setting up a company in Nepal walks through the incorporation step by step.

A worked example

An NRN in the United States wants to buy 30% of an existing Nepali software company. Because the sector is open and the investment meets the threshold, the route is manageable. He starts by confirming eligibility, then files for foreign investment approval, then subscribes to new shares. The capital enters through his bank, not hand to hand, and is recorded at the central bank. Two years later, when he wants to repatriate a dividend, the paper trail from that original transfer is what makes the remittance smooth. An NRN who wires money informally in year one often finds the same funds impossible to send back in year three.

Repatriation of profits and capital

Profits, dividends and, on winding up, capital can be repatriated subject to Nepal Rastra Bank approval and the company's tax obligations. The key is documentation: funds should enter through the banking system and the equity should be reflected in the company's records. Keep your NRN status and papers current, because repatriation depends on being able to show exactly where the money came from.

Common pitfalls

  • Committing to a sector that is closed to foreign investment.
  • Bringing funds in informally, which then blocks repatriation.
  • Skipping notarisation and authentication, causing delays at the registrar or the bank.
  • Confusing company registration with foreign investment approval, when both are required.

Frequently asked questions

Can an NRN own 100% of a Nepali company? In sectors not on the negative list, generally yes.

Is the minimum investment lower for NRNs? Sometimes, depending on the sector and the type of investment. Confirm the current policy before structuring.

Can an NRN invest while living abroad? Yes, largely. Notarised and authenticated documents and a local representative allow most of the process to be handled remotely.

Can an NRN repatriate profits? Yes, after tax clearance and Nepal Rastra Bank approval, provided the original investment was documented.

Does an NRN need foreign investment approval? Yes. NRNs are treated as foreign investors under FITTA and require approval.

Can an NRN buy land in Nepal? An NRN who holds Nepali citizenship generally can. An NRN who has taken foreign citizenship faces the same property restrictions as other foreign nationals. See our guide on foreigners buying property.

title: Can Foreigners Buy Property in Nepal? The Rules Explained
content:
Foreigners are often surprised by how much of the answer to this question depends on what they actually want the property for. Owning the land outright and having secure, long-term use of it are two different things in Nepal, and the law treats them very differently. Understanding that distinction early saves both money and heartache.

This guide explains what a foreign national can and cannot do with property in Nepal, and the routes that genuinely work.

Quick answer

In general, a foreign national cannot own land in Nepal in their own name. Land ownership is reserved for Nepali citizens. There is no simple path to individual freehold ownership for a foreigner. That does not close the door on property altogether. Foreign-invested businesses can lease, can hold property for their own operations in eligible circumstances, and in narrow situations can buy apartments. The structure you choose matters far more here than in most countries.

The legal position

Nepal's land rules reserve ownership to Nepali citizens. A foreign individual buying land in their own name is not viable, and arrangements that try to hold land through a local nominee carry serious legal and reputational risk, including the risk that the nominee's own creditors or heirs take the land. The workable routes for a foreign national or a foreign company are leasing, corporate holding in eligible circumstances, and limited apartment ownership.

Option 1: Long-term leasing

For a foreign business that needs premises, a registered lease is the most common and safest route. Foreign-invested companies use commercial leases for offices, restaurants, factories and hotels. Register the lease so it is secure, and set the terms, permitted use and renewal rights out precisely. Leasing gives you reliable use of the property for the term without the complications of ownership. For a twenty-year industrial lease, the lease document is effectively your asset, and it deserves the same care as a purchase deed.

Option 2: A foreign-invested company holding property

A company incorporated in Nepal, even with foreign shareholders, is a Nepali legal entity. In eligible circumstances it can acquire and hold property for its own business operations. This route is regulated and depends on the sector and the nature of the use, so it should be structured with advice rather than assumed. The important point is that the company holds the property, not the foreign shareholder personally. If you sell your shares, you sell the company that owns the land, which is a different transaction with different tax consequences.

Option 3: Apartments and residential ownership

Specific rules allow foreign nationals to purchase apartments and flats in limited situations, but the conditions are narrow and often misunderstood. Availability depends on your citizenship and residency status and on the particular development. Confirm the current position before any purchase commitment, because a scheme that sounds straightforward can turn out not to apply to you.

A worked example

A foreign investor wants a home in Kathmandu and a factory outside it. The home is the harder problem. Rather than attempting ownership through a Nepali friend, which would leave the investment exposed, the practical route is a long registered lease or an apartment under the limited framework, whichever fits. The factory is different: the investor's Nepali company can hold industrial land for its own operations where the sector and use qualify. Two goals, two structures, and getting them the wrong way round is the classic mistake.

What every buyer or lessee should verify first

  • Confirm the land record (kitta) at the land revenue office shows the correct owner.
  • Check for mortgages, loans and other encumbrances.
  • Verify the land category and any public restrictions.
  • Confirm the tax and valuation position before registration.

A clean title check before you commit is the cheapest protection any property transaction can buy.

Can an NRN buy property in Nepal?

Non-resident Nepalis are treated differently. An NRN who remains a Nepali citizen can generally acquire property, and many NRNs buy land or a house for family use or investment. An NRN who has taken foreign citizenship faces the same restrictions as any other foreign national. Because citizenship, not residency, decides your rights, this is the first point to clarify with a lawyer before you negotiate anything.

Practical steps

  1. Establish your legal capacity to own or lease before negotiating.
  2. Run the title, encumbrance and land-category checks at the relevant office.
  3. Structure the deal through a registered lease or a corporate entity, with advice.
  4. Prepare and register the deed or lease, and pay the applicable taxes and fees.
  5. Update the records so the transaction is reflected at the land office.

Frequently asked questions

Can a foreigner buy land in Nepal? Generally no. Land ownership is reserved for Nepali citizens.

Can a foreigner buy an apartment in Nepal? In limited situations, under specific rules, depending on citizenship, residency and the development. This should be confirmed case by case.

Can a foreign company own property in Nepal? A Nepali company with foreign shareholders can hold property for its own operations in eligible circumstances. The company owns it, not the foreign shareholder.

Is leasing a safe alternative? Yes. A registered long-term lease is the most common and safest route for a foreign business.

Can an NRN own property? An NRN who holds Nepali citizenship generally can. One who has taken foreign citizenship cannot, on the same terms as other foreigners.

What happens if I buy through a Nepali nominee? It is legally risky and can result in the loss of the property if the nominee's circumstances change. We advise against it.

title: PAN and VAT Registration in Nepal: What Businesses Need to Know
content:
Of all the post-incorporation steps, PAN and VAT cause the most needless difficulty. Neither is complicated on its own. What catches founders out is the timing, and the fact that a company's tax responsibilities begin on the day of incorporation, whether or not it has earned a rupee. A company that treats tax registration as a task for "later" usually ends up paying for the delay, either in penalties or in invoices a customer cannot use.

This guide explains what PAN and VAT are, when each applies, and how to get both right from day one.

Quick answer

Every company in Nepal needs a Permanent Account Number (PAN), issued by the Inland Revenue Department. Businesses whose taxable turnover crosses the legal threshold must also register for Value Added Tax (VAT). A company's PAN is obtained soon after incorporation and quickly. VAT registration, and the separate registration of each branch, are the steps first-time founders most often miss.

What a PAN is

The PAN is the tax identification number for individuals and businesses in Nepal. Companies obtain it as a post-incorporation step, typically within a short window of receiving the certificate of incorporation. Salaried employees, landlords and self-employed professionals also hold personal PANs for withholding and filing. The number attaches to the person or entity, not to a trade name, so a company that later changes its name keeps its PAN.

What VAT registration is

VAT applies once taxable turnover reaches the legal threshold, and registration is completed at the Inland Revenue Office. Once registered, the business charges VAT on its sales and claims input VAT on its purchases, filing periodic returns to settle the difference. Businesses below the threshold may register voluntarily, and many B2B suppliers do, because it lets their customers claim input credit on the invoices they receive. For a business selling mainly to other registered businesses, voluntary registration is often a commercial advantage rather than a burden.

Documents you will need

  • The certificate of incorporation, or the registration certificate for another entity type
  • The memorandum and articles of association, where applicable
  • Details of the business premises, including address and ownership or rental documents
  • Identification of the authorised representatives and directors
  • The business bank account details

The steps for a new company

  1. Incorporate with the Office of the Company Registrar.
  2. Apply for the PAN at the Inland Revenue Office soon after incorporation.
  3. Register for VAT once turnover will cross the threshold, or apply voluntarily.
  4. Register each branch or permanent establishment separately.
  5. Build the PAN and VAT numbers into invoices, contracts and accounts from day one.

A worked example

A technology consultancy incorporates in Kathmandu and plans to bill clients in Nepal and abroad. Because most of its clients are VAT-registered businesses that want input credit, the firm registers for VAT voluntarily even before crossing the threshold. Its PAN is issued within days of incorporation, and the same numbers appear on every invoice. Later, when the consultancy opens a second office in Pokhara, it knows the branch must be registered separately. A competitor that waits until turnover forces the issue finds that invoices issued in the meantime cannot support the customer's input claim, leaving an awkward hole in its early bookkeeping.

Consequences of late registration

Operating without a PAN where one is required attracts penalties, and VAT carries the same risk. Late VAT registration also means the business could not issue valid VAT invoices for the period before registration, which complicates both customer billing and input claims. Because the tax obligations of a company run from incorporation even before revenue begins, registering early is cheaper and simpler than catching up.

Annual compliance after registration

With PAN and VAT in place, the ongoing obligations begin: periodic VAT returns, social security contributions if you employ staff, and the annual corporate income tax return supported by audited financial statements. Missing a filing date attracts fines quickly and invites scrutiny. Most businesses keep a compliance calendar from the start rather than tracking deadlines by memory.

Frequently asked questions

Is PAN registration mandatory for every company? Yes. Every company in Nepal must obtain a PAN.

When must a company get its PAN? Soon after incorporation, within the short window set by the Inland Revenue Department.

When does VAT registration become mandatory? Once taxable turnover reaches the legal threshold. Below it, registration is voluntary but often worthwhile for B2B suppliers.

Can I register for VAT voluntarily? Yes. Many businesses do, so their customers can claim input credit.

Does each branch need its own registration? Yes. Each branch or permanent establishment is registered separately for VAT.

What happens if I register late? Penalties apply, and invoices issued before registration cannot support a customer's VAT claim.

How often are VAT returns filed? Returns are filed on a periodic cycle, commonly monthly, depending on the registration. Confirm the cycle that applies to you and build it into your calendar.

title: Bail in Nepal: How to Apply and What the Court Considers
content:
When someone is arrested in Nepal, the hours that follow decide more about the case than almost anything that comes later. Families usually call a lawyer in a state of alarm, unsure whether bail is even possible and what it would take. The honest answer is that bail is the default for many offences, but not all, and the difference lies in how the case is classified and how the application is made.

This guide explains how bail works, what the court weighs, and what to do in the first critical window.

Quick answer

Bail is the legal route to release from custody while a case is pending. It is not automatic, but it is the norm where the offence is not serious and the accused is not a flight risk. The court considers the nature of the offence, the strength of the evidence, the risk of flight or witness interference, and any prior record. How quickly bail is granted depends on the court, the classification of the offence, and how well the application is presented.

How bail works

Bail is decided by the court handling the case. At the early stage, the question of release is normally considered when the case first comes before the court after arrest. The court weighs how serious the offence is, how strong the evidence appears, whether the accused might flee or interfere with witnesses, and whether there is a criminal record. For minor offences the accused is usually released on bail, or where no remand is warranted, on a simple recognisance.

When bail is routinely available

  • Offences classified as not serious, where the accused is unlikely to interfere with the case.
  • Where the accused has no criminal record and a fixed residence in Nepal.
  • Where detention has run past the legal limit without a proper extension.

When bail is harder to obtain

For serious offences, particularly those carrying long prison terms, bail is opposed and the court scrutinises the evidence closely. In these cases the onus shifts to showing why the accused should be released, and the application must answer the court's specific concerns rather than repeat general arguments.

What the court expects from an application

  1. Identify the correct court and file promptly, with the specific facts of the case.
  2. Address the recognised factors: seriousness, evidence, flight risk and witness interference.
  3. Offer conditions that reassure the court, such as a fixed residence, regular attendance, and a suitable surety.
  4. Attend the hearing on the fixed date and respond to any objection.

A worked example

A foreign businessperson is detained after a commercial dispute is reported as fraud. The first instinct, to explain everything to the police, is the wrong one. Instead, the person confirms identity, asks for a lawyer, and says nothing further. The lawyer files a bail application that directly addresses the court's likely concern, that a foreign national might leave the country, by offering a local address, a passport deposit and a Nepali surety. Framing the application around that single worry is what gets the release. A generic application, filed a week later, often does not.

If bail is refused

A refusal is not the end. Depending on the stage, the decision can be challenged by a review before the same court, an application to a higher court, or a writ petition. Timing matters, because the review window is short and the longer a person stays in custody the harder the case becomes. Someone who tracks the deadlines in the file is essential at this point.

What to do immediately after an arrest

The period between arrest and the first court appearance is the most consequential part of any case. The accused should avoid statements beyond confirming identity, should exercise the right to a lawyer, and should not agree to anything under pressure. Anything said at the police stage can resurface at trial, so the discipline shown in the first 48 hours often sets the course of the whole case.

White-collar and corporate cases

In fraud, money-laundering and regulatory matters the bail analysis is different again. These cases often turn on documentary evidence, the nature of the financial harm, and the risk that a financially mobile accused might abscond. A company facing a regulatory and criminal investigation at the same time should treat its defence as a single strategy from day one rather than responding piecemeal.

Frequently asked questions

Is bail a right in Nepal? It is the norm for non-serious offences, but it is not automatic. The court decides based on the offence, the evidence and the risk factors.

How quickly can bail be granted? It is usually considered at the first appearance after arrest. A well-prepared application filed promptly improves the chances of an early release.

Can a foreign national get bail in Nepal? Yes, though flight risk is examined closely. Offering a local address, a passport deposit and a Nepali surety helps.

What if bail is denied? It can be challenged by review, by application to a higher court, or by writ petition, depending on the stage. The review window is short.

Should the accused speak to the police? Beyond confirming identity, no. Statements made at the police stage can be used at trial.

Does a prior record affect bail? Yes. A prior record weighs against release, particularly for similar offences.

title: Company Registration in Nepal: Costs, Documents and Timeline
content:
Most founders arrive in Nepal expecting the hard part to be the registration itself. In practice, the registration is the easy part. It usually takes days. What surprises people is everything around it: clearing a name that satisfies the registrar, opening a corporate bank account, and, for foreign investors, a separate investment approval that sits before the company can even be incorporated.

This guide explains the whole picture in plain terms, so you know what you are committing to before you start.

Quick answer

A private limited company is registered at the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR) under the Companies Act, 2063. For a straightforward domestic company, the paperwork is light, the government fees are modest, and incorporation can be done in days once the name is cleared. Add PAN and VAT, a bank account and any sector licence, and the realistic timeline is three to six weeks. If there is foreign investment involved, a further approval stage applies before incorporation, and we cover that separately in our guide for foreign investors.

Which company type fits you?

The structure you choose affects cost, compliance and how easily you can raise money later. Most businesses fall into one of four buckets.

A private limited company is the default. Shareholders' liability is limited, the company is a separate legal person, and the number of shareholders is capped, with no public offering. It suits virtually every startup, trading business, consultancy and foreign subsidiary.

A public limited company is for larger businesses that intend to raise capital from the public. The regulation and reporting are heavier, so it rarely makes sense at the start.

A not-for-profit company is used for non-profit objectives. This is different from the NGO route, which is governed by separate social-welfare law.

A branch or liaison office lets a foreign company operate in Nepal without incorporating a local subsidiary. A branch can trade; a liaison office cannot. Both need approval from the Department of Industry first.

The registration process, step by step

Name clearance. The proposed name is submitted to the OCR for availability. Names that are too close to an existing company, or that mislead, are rejected, which is the most common reason founders are sent back to the start. It is worth preparing two or three alternatives.

Draft the constitutional documents. The memorandum and articles of association set out the name, objectives, capital, shareholders and governance. These documents govern how the company runs, so the drafting deserves attention now, not later when a dispute forces the question.

Filing and registration. The incorporation application and documents are filed with the OCR. Once approved, the certificate of incorporation issues and the company exists as a legal person.

Tax registration. The company obtains a Permanent Account Number from the Inland Revenue Office and registers for VAT if it expects to cross the turnover threshold.

Bank account. The corporate bank account is opened, and where foreign investment is involved, the capital is remitted through banking channels and recorded at Nepal Rastra Bank.

Sector approvals. If the business is an industry, it registers with the Department of Industry. Sector licences, such as those for tourism or education, are obtained where they apply.

What it costs

The government side is genuinely modest: a name-clearance application fee, a registration fee based on authorised capital, and a small PAN registration charge. Authorised capital drives the registration fee, and setting it higher than you need means paying more for no benefit.

The larger line item is professional fees. These vary with the capital structure, the drafting required, and the sector approvals involved, and we agree them up front before any work starts. For a foreign-owned company, the separate investment approval adds both time and cost to the file.

How long it takes

Stage Realistic duration
Name clearance One to three days
Document preparation Three to seven days
Registration at the OCR A few days to two weeks
PAN and VAT One to two days
Bank account Three to five days
Total Three to six weeks

Foreign investment cases run longer, because the approval stage comes first. Expect several weeks to a couple of months depending on the sector.

Documents you will need

  • Citizenship, passport or company documents for every shareholder and director
  • The proposed company name and registered office address
  • The memorandum and articles of association
  • Details of authorised and issued capital
  • Identification and PAN details of the directors
  • For a foreign parent, a board resolution authorising the subsidiary

A worked example

Two founders, one based in Kathmandu and one in Dubai, want to set up an IT services company. Because the Dubai founder is a foreign investor, the process starts not at the OCR but at the Department of Industry, where the investment is approved. Only then is the company incorporated, capital is remitted through banking channels and recorded at Nepal Rastra Bank, and PAN and VAT follow. The Kathmandu founder's citizenship documents handle the local side, while the Dubai founder's documents are apostilled and translated. Had they incorporated first in the belief that registration came before approval, they would have had to redo the memorandum to match an approval that arrived later.

Life after incorporation

Incorporation is the beginning of compliance, not the end. The company must keep statutory registers, hold board and general meetings, maintain share records, and file annual returns. This is the work that quietly slips in year one, and it is exactly when slip-ups become expensive to correct. Putting the statutory calendar in place early avoids that.

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to register a company in Nepal? Once the name is cleared and documents are ready, registration itself is quick. The full set-up, including PAN, VAT, the bank account and any sector approvals, is realistically three to six weeks.

Can one person own a company? Yes. A private limited company can be formed with a single shareholder.

Is there a minimum capital requirement? There is no fixed minimum for an ordinary private company. Capital should be realistic and aligned with the business, and higher authorised capital means higher registration fees.

Can a foreigner register a company in Nepal? Yes, but a foreign investor needs approval under the foreign investment law before incorporation. See our FDI guide for the full sequence.

What is the difference between authorised and issued capital? Authorised capital is the maximum the company may issue; issued capital is what shareholders have actually subscribed. The registration fee follows authorised capital.

Do I need to be physically present? Not necessarily. A power of attorney lets a representative file on your behalf, though banking formalities often require the directors in person.

What happens if I ignore annual compliance? Late filings attract penalties, and persistent non-compliance can lead to the company being struck off. It is far cheaper to keep the calendar current than to fix a lapse later.

title: Obtaining Business Licences and Approvals in Nepal
content:
Company registration is where a business in Nepal begins, but it is rarely where compliance ends. Almost every worthwhile activity carries a second layer: an operating licence, a sector permit, or an approval that gives you the standing to actually do the work. Banks, landlords, buyers and regulators all look for these documents, and a missing one tends to surface at the worst possible moment, often when a payment, an import or a deal depends on it.

This guide explains how to work out which licences apply to you, and how to keep them current.

Quick answer

Beyond incorporation, most businesses need one or more operating licences or sector approvals. Which ones apply depends on what you sell and where you operate. The practical approach is to map your activity against the responsible ministries and departments first, apply to the right authority the first time, and then track renewals so nothing lapses.

Why the second layer exists

Incorporation makes a company exist. Licences make it lawful to do a particular thing. A company can be perfectly incorporated and still be unable to serve food, import goods, build a structure or operate a clinic without the specific permission for that activity. Regulators in Nepal are activity-based, so the licence follows the work, not the entity.

Working out what applies to you

The answer depends on your sector. A few examples show the pattern:

  • A restaurant needs a hygiene permit and, if it serves alcohol, a liquor licence.
  • A manufacturer needs industry registration and environmental clearances.
  • An importer needs an import authorisation tied to its PAN and VAT accounts.
  • A tourism business needs registration with the relevant tourism authority.
  • A healthcare provider needs sector approval from the health regulator.

The practical method is to list what your business will actually do, then match each activity to the department or agency responsible for it. Doing that mapping before you open avoids applying to the wrong office and discovering the error through a refusal.

Getting the application right the first time

Most licence delays are document delays. Applications stall because a supporting paper is missing, a fee was paid to the wrong office, or a form was completed for the wrong category. Preparing a complete file, with the correct fee and the right category, is what turns a weeks-long process into a short one. Where approvals depend on one another, the sequence matters as much as the papers.

Renewals and the calendar

Licences expire. Some renew annually, others on a fixed cycle, and the penalty for a lapse is not only a fine. An expired permit can suspend your ability to operate, freeze a payment, or block a transaction while a buyer waits for proof that you are compliant. Mapping every licence to its renewal date, and starting each renewal in good time, is the simplest protection a business can put in place.

A worked example

A foreign-invested company opens a boutique hotel. Incorporation and PAN are straightforward, and the owners assume the rest will follow. But the hotel needs a tourism registration, a municipal business registration, a hygiene permit for its kitchen and a liquor licence for its bar. Each sits with a different authority. Because the owners mapped the licences before opening, the kitchen and bar were compliant on day one. Had they opened first and sorted the paperwork later, the first inspection would have closed the bar and the delay would have cost far more than the licences themselves.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need more than company registration? Usually yes. Most activities need at least one operating licence or sector approval on top of incorporation.

How do I know which licences apply to me? Map what your business actually does against the responsible ministries and departments, then apply accordingly.

Can I operate while a licence is pending? Generally no, for the licensed activity. Operating without it risks fines and closure.

Do licences expire? Yes. Renewal cycles vary, so track each licence to its due date.

What happens if a licence lapses? Penalties apply, and operations for the licensed activity may have to stop until it is restored.

Is this different for foreign-invested companies? The licences are activity-based and apply to any company, though foreign investment adds its own approval layer.

title: Real Estate Licensing and Project Approvals in Nepal
content:
Land in Nepal is rarely bought or developed on title alone. Behind every project that actually gets built sit land-use and zoning rules, building permits, developer registrations and, for larger or commercial projects, approvals at the municipal and sometimes central level. A missing layer rarely announces itself at the start. It surfaces later, as a hard stop when a completion certificate, a sale registration or a mortgage is on the line.

This guide explains the approvals that matter most for a property project in Nepal, and the order in which they should be secured.

Quick answer

Real estate projects in Nepal require land-use and zoning compliance, building permits before construction, developer registration and project approval for advertised or sold units, and, for larger or commercial schemes, further municipal or central approvals. Buyers should also complete a title and boundary verification. Securing these in the right order is what keeps a project deliverable.

The approvals that matter most

  • Land-use and zoning compliance, confirming the land may lawfully be used for the intended purpose.
  • Building permits, obtained before construction begins.
  • Developer registration and project approval, confirmed before units are advertised or sold.
  • Title and boundary verification, so a buyer knows exactly what is being acquired.

Each one depends on the integrity of the last. A building permit issued on land that cannot lawfully be used for that purpose is worthless when a buyer's lender examines the file.

Why the sequence matters

Property approvals in Nepal form a chain, not a checklist. Land-use comes before design, design before the building permit, and the permit before construction. A developer who starts building while a permit is pending is not merely late. The construction may be unauthorised, and remedying that can mean demolition or a costly regularisation process. Doing the steps in order is faster than doing them out of order and repairing the consequences.

For developers

A developer should confirm zoning and land-use first, secure the building permit before breaking ground, and register the developer and obtain project approval before advertising or selling any unit. Where a project is financed, lenders will examine the whole chain, from land rights to permits, before releasing funds. A clean chain is what makes a project fundable and saleable.

A worked example

Two developers start projects on adjacent plots. The first confirms zoning, finalises the design to match the permitted use, and takes the building permit before construction. The second, eager to move, begins construction while the permit is pending and discovers the design breaches a setback rule. The first reaches completion and sells units with clean paperwork. The second faces rework, a fresh approval cycle and nervous buyers. The land and the market were the same. The difference was the order of the approvals.

For buyers

A buyer's protection comes from verification before commitment. Complete a title and boundary check so you know the seller owns what is being sold, that the land is not encumbered, and that the boundaries match the deed. Whether you are buying a completed unit or land to develop, this check is the cheapest insurance available.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a building permit before construction? Yes. Construction should not begin before the building permit is issued.

What is land-use or zoning compliance? Confirmation that the land may lawfully be used for the intended purpose.

Does a developer need to be registered? Yes. A developer should be registered and the project approved before units are advertised or sold.

What should a buyer verify? Title, encumbrances and boundaries, through a proper title and boundary check before committing.

Can approvals be obtained after construction? It is risky and often impossible to regularise. Obtaining them in order is far safer.

Do commercial projects need extra approvals? Larger or commercial projects typically require additional municipal, and sometimes central, approvals.

title: Business Approvals Every Company in Nepal Should Track
content:
Once a company is incorporated in Nepal, its obligations multiply quietly. PAN and VAT registrations, provident fund and social security enrolment, municipal business registration, and any industry-specific permits begin landing on different calendars, each with its own deadline and penalty clock. None of them is hard on its own. Together, they are exactly the kind of administrative load that slips when a business is busy growing.

This guide explains why a compliance calendar is one of the most useful things a company can build, and what belongs on it.

Quick answer

After incorporation, a company in Nepal faces a recurring set of registrations, filings and renewals, each handled by a different authority and each with its own due date. A compliance calendar that maps every obligation to its deadline turns a scattered set of risks into a manageable routine. The approach is simple: list every obligation, assign each a date and an owner, and review the calendar regularly.

The obligations that build up

  • PAN registration, and VAT registration where applicable.
  • Periodic VAT returns and the annual corporate income tax return.
  • Social security and provident fund enrolment and contributions.
  • Municipal business registration.
  • Industry-specific permits and their renewals.
  • Annual filings at the Office of the Company Registrar.

Individually these are routine. Collectively, they are the reason so many businesses discover a problem only after a deadline has passed.

Why the calendar matters

The companies that run into trouble are rarely the ones with a single large problem. More often they are the ones where a renewal lapsed, a filing was missed by two days, or a permit expired in the middle of signing a contract. A missed date is rarely catastrophic on its own, but the penalty, the reinstatement and the disruption to a live transaction can easily outweigh the cost of the underlying obligation many times over. A calendar changes the arithmetic.

What belongs on the calendar

  1. Every registration, with the date it was obtained and any renewal date.
  2. Every recurring filing, with its frequency and due date.
  3. Every contribution obligation, such as social security, with its payment cycle.
  4. Every permit, with its expiry and the lead time needed to renew.
  5. The owner of each item, so responsibility is clear.

A worked example

A trading company is doing well and lands a large supply contract. At the signing, the buyer asks for proof of current VAT registration and a valid import authorisation. Both are technically held, but the import authorisation expired three weeks earlier and was never renewed. The buyer pauses the contract while the company scrambles to reinstate the permit. The company lost nothing it could not fix, but it lost time, credibility and, briefly, the deal. A calendar that flagged the expiry six weeks earlier would have prevented the entire episode.

Keeping the calendar current

A calendar is only useful if it is reviewed. Set a regular moment, monthly or quarterly, to look ahead at the coming period, confirm nothing has lapsed, and start renewals early. When a new obligation appears, whether from a new licence or a new sector, add it immediately rather than trying to remember it later.

Frequently asked questions

Why do I need a compliance calendar? Because obligations fall on different authorities and dates, and missed deadlines carry penalties that are easy to avoid.

What should be on it? Registrations, recurring filings, contribution obligations, permit expiries and renewals, and the owner of each item.

How often should it be reviewed? At least monthly or quarterly, with renewals started well before their due date.

What happens if a filing is missed? Penalties apply, and some activities cannot continue until the lapse is corrected.

Is this only for large companies? No. Small companies face the same obligations and have less margin for error.

Can these tasks be delegated? Yes. Many businesses appoint a professional to build and maintain the calendar and handle the filings.
